title: Neocloud Shakeout Looms, and Nvidia Has a Lot to Lose
content: How many young AI cloud providers can the market, and Nvidia, support? That’s one of the big questions after a week in which investors worried about the data center buildout and the risks that its unproven participants, known as neoclouds, are taking. Those risks include loading up on debt (CoreWeave) or trying to go public without much of a track record (Firmus and Nscale). Firmus abruptly pulled its public offering last week while shares of CoreWeave and its smaller rivals fell around 20%. The concerns even hit bigger AI cloud providers like Oracle. Data center and neocloud executives told me there’s a limit to the number of AI cloud providers that can exist, even if Nvidia provides many of them with investment or backstops.

title: Why Upstart Banks May Have to Keep Raising Money
content: The Trump administration has opened the door for entrepreneurs to start new banks in the U.S., many funded by venture capital. But there’s a catch for fast-growing newcomers. Upstarts like Palmer Luckey’s Erebor Bank, as well as other new entrants like Openreserve and Augustus, will likely have to keep raising money as they grow to maintain the capital cushion they need to satisfy bank regulatory requirements. That’s a contrast to most startups, which use fresh venture money to pay for operating expenses and expand the business. Regulators require banks to maintain a capital cushion to absorb potential losses and protect depositors. That cushion is typically measured through a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio, which measures a bank’s capital relative to assets including cash, loans and investments. For instance, a bank subject to a 12% minimum tier 1 leverage ratio needs to maintain at least $12 in capital for every $100 in assets. As a bank attracts more deposits, its assets, such as loans, typically grow too, increasing the amount of capital it needs to meet that minimum ratio. Established banks can build up their capital through their profits, but newer banks that aren’t yet profitable have to rely instead on raising fresh equity from investors. Startup banks have already been raising significant funding to get their businesses off the ground or as deposits grow. Erebor Bank is set to raise $1.5 billion in a fresh fundraising round at an $8 billion valuation before the investment, after launching with $625 million in committed capital in February. The fundraising comes as the bank has seen its deposits surge to $7 billion as of the end of September, up from $4 billion at the end of the prior quarter. Meanwhile, Openreserve, an a16z crypto-backed bank that raised $25 million in September, said it expects to announce an additional capital raise to meet its regulatory requirements ahead of its planned opening early next year. Then there’s Augustus, a startup bank focused on serving fintech companies. It raised $180 million in a Tiger Global Management–led round in July at a $1 billion valuation and expects to open later this year. Regulators give capital ratios to each bank based on their assessment of the institution’s business plans and risks. Newly created banks typically face tougher capital requirements than established banks. For the first three years of operation, Erebor and Openreserve must each maintain a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio of 12%, while Augustus faces a 10% minimum. Established banks, by comparison, typically have ratios of between 5% and 6%. “There’s no question that the regulators treat de novo banks—new banks—differently than they do well-established banks,” according to Brian Graham, a partner and co-founder at consulting firm Klaros Group who advises clients on bank charter applications. Graham noted that the extra capital requirements typically go away after a bank has been operating for three years. The upstart banks are generally pursuing relatively new business models or focusing on sectors big banks typically avoid. Erebor Bank, for example, has gained traction in areas prioritized by the Trump administration, such as defense startups and crypto firms, and is expanding in geographies traditional banks typically avoid, including Venezuela and Syria. In addition to making minimum capital requirements, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.—a banking regulator—imposed an unusual condition on its approval of Erebor for the deposit insurance program. Under a capital-call provision, Erebor’s investors must contribute additional capital if the bank doesn’t meet its minimum capital requirements, according to a filing. The filing didn’t disclose which investors are required to provide the capital backstop. In the meantime, upstart banks that are looking to drive revenue growth from lending rather than fees will likely need to tap investors to build their capital. “To the extent the bank’s business model is reliant materially on the balance sheet for revenue and net income, you’re going to need to raise more capital to drive growth,” Klaros’ Graham said. Openreserve, for its part, plans to make loans backed by traditional assets and turn them into digital tokens that can trade on blockchain, potentially providing a new source of loans for investors and lenders in the crypto market. For example, it plans to lend businesses money against their trade receivables, turning those assets into digital tokens to make them easier to trade. “Our ambition is to be the on-chain GSIB,” referring to a globally systemically important bank, said Dee Choubey, founder and CEO of Openreserve. The bank also plans to issue its own stablecoin and to offer tokenized deposits, digital versions of traditional bank accounts that earn interest. Over time, it aims to provide banking and payment services to other digital banks. Augustus plans to focus on helping fintech, crypto and remittance companies move money across borders using both traditional banking systems and stablecoins. That will put it in competition with existing banks like United Texas Bank, which has become dominant in processing dollar payments for overseas crypto exchanges. “Whenever someone outside the U.S. touches the dollar through a local bank or local fintech, that always has to be facilitated by a U.S. nationally chartered clearing bank, so we provide that service,” said Augustus CEO Ferdinand Dabitz. In Europe, the bank already counts crypto exchange Kraken among its clients. Augustus is less focused on activities like lending, however, and has a lower ratio than the other two. The company has raised significantly more than its initial capital requirement, which could lessen the need for more fundraising in the near term. “We are less focused on the credit side as other market participants. We think the clearing side is really where we shine,” Dabitz said. title: PGE gets it: electric semi trucks provide HEAVY DUTY backup for the grid [video]
content:
Commercial EVs
Electric Semi Truck
Electrical grid
Jo Borrás
| Oct 18 2026 - 8:17 am PT
Oregon utility Portland General Electric (“PGE”) is highlighting the environmental, health, and grid benefits to electrifying medium- and heavy-duty commercial trucks, calling the battery-backed big rigs “batteries on wheels.”
Earlier this month, Oregon hosted its first, fleet-focused electric ride-and-drive event, bringing everything from Class 8 electric semi trucks and medium-duty “last mile” delivery trucks to battery-powered equipment assets like
wheel loaders
excavators
together in one place so the state’s fleet operators (and fleet buyers) could experience the latest generation of commercial EVs for themselves.
More importantly, Portland utility PGE was also on-hand, along with local NBC News affiliate KGW8, to address one of the most prevalent myths spread by EV detractors:
the one that says EVs can overload the energy grid
PGE transportation electrification manager Karla Hendrickson shut that nonsense down decisively, touting the electric trucks’ ability to help support the grid during peak load events and calling them out as, “
grid ready assets
,” capable of helping the utility manage periods of high electricity demand while keeping costs low. “Electric school buses are particularly intriguing,” adds said Hendrickson. “Their schedules are predictable and they can spend long stretches parked.”
PGE is already testing the ability to dispatch energy from the state’s deployed fleet of school buses back to the grid.
Big rig, big battery
There are nearly 150,000 registered EVs operating on Oregon roads today, but while the push for electric passenger vehicles gains steam and the electric charging infrastructure to support them is being built out along the state’s travel corridors,
the push to electrify medium- and heavy-duty commercial vehicles is just getting started
As it gains steam, the push to electrify these vehicles could give the utility access to more stored energy, keeping ratepayers’ bills low,
insulating fleets from the wild swings of diesel fuel prices
, and (of course) help
Oregoons
Oregonians breathe a bit easier. Literally.
“These heavy trucks and buses represent a relatively small amount of the fleet of vehicles on the road in Oregon,” explains Gerick Kransky, with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality. “But they represent a disproportionate amount of the emissions that we deal with from transportation.”

title: Tiny Titan: new residential battery system from EcoFlow starts small
content:
Solar power
home battery
Jo Borrás
| Oct 18 2026 - 7:42 am PT
EcoFlow is hoping to make a titanic splash with its new, smaller (but scalable!) residential energy storage lineup that the company is calling a more approachable entry point to its backup battery offerings.
EcoFlow’s new, three-model Titan 5000 range of home backup batteries starts off relatively small with “just” a single, 5 kWh energy storage module that’s enough to keep your refrigerator, lights and Wi-Fi going while keeping your phone and laptop batteries charged. That’s just the start, however, as the system is designed to easily scale up with the addition of more 5,000 Wh modules (hence, the name) to meet your more substantial energy needs — all the way up to 30 kWh.
The company says that’s enough juice to keep an average US home humming along for a full two days without grid power; and that power will (obviis)
last a lot longer if you can keep the HVAC system off and keep energy use to a minimum
Keep it simple
Titan 5000; via EcoFlow.
All three Titan models start with a 5 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO₄) battery and can be expanded to the previously mentioned 30 kWh maximum capacity by stacking more modular batteries, but they differ in output power and capacity for solar panel system integration.
The entry-spec Titan 5000 Classic delivers up to 4 kW of 120V output
, while the Titan 5000 steps that up to 7.2 kW continuous power with both 120V and 240V split-phase output available.
The flagship Titan 5000 Plus, meanwhile, also promises 7.2 kW of continuous power, but can reach up to 10 kW of peak power when paired with solar, thanks to EcoFlow’s X-Fusion 2.0 PV Boost technology. The Titan 5000 and Plus can also pair with the
EcoFlow Smart Home Panel 10
, which the company claims can help homeowners add backup power without replacing their main electrical panel or enduring a lengthy, complex installation.
“Whole-home backup has traditionally required households to choose between the power they want and the cost and complexity they’re willing to take on,” explains Brian Essenmacher, Head of US Business Development at EcoFlow. “With TITAN,
we’re giving more families a practical way to get the power they need
, while also helping them manage energy more intelligently every day.”
EcoFlow is allowing “early bird”
the chance to lock in one of three bundle deals now with a $50 pre-payment
, saving up to $2,999 in November when it officially releases (and when they’ll be expected pay the remaining balance). It’s worth noting, too, that the FCC authorizations for all three of EcoFlow’s new Titan 5000 systems are dated July 20, before the FCC’s July 28 restrictions on foreign-produced inverters kicked in.

content:

| Oct 18 2026 - 6:38 am PT
Chinese PV and solar equipment brand LEAPTING has taken the wraps off its new, battery-powered Auto-Navigation Forklift Robot (AFR) designed to speed up the installation of large,
utility-scale solar power projects
The newest member in a growing lineup of fully autonomous solar construction and maintenance robots
, the latest LEAPTING AFR was revealed earlier this week at a solar technology conference in Dubai, where the heavy-duty, fully autonomous and battery-powered tracked
forklift
was called the “missing link” in solar material handling for its ability to delivers solar module pallets directly from terminals or laydown yards to installation rows without the need to put either a human operator or flagman in harm’s way.
“The AFR combines GPS-RTK, laser-based simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and 3D computer vision to locate pallets, identify fork-hole coordinates in real time, and auto-plan insertion paths,” the company said, in a statement. “
It further features 360-degree multi-line LiDAR
, intelligent obstacle avoidance, and a three-tier braking system.”
The thing, itself
Image by LEAPTING.
The AFR uses a 48 V, 400 Ah lithium battery with a nominal capacity of 19.2 kWh, sending power to a pair of electric drive motors mounted high in the track. The combination is reportedly good for about 10 total hp and a full eight hours of continuous operation under “standard” operating conditions – more than enough, in other words, to handle a full day’s work.
And, thanks to its IP67 all-weather protection and fully tracked, tank-like mobility, the all-terrain LEAPTING forklift robot can handle 3,000 kg (~6,600 lbs.) of solar and PV materials per load across some of the most demanding job sites you can think, from desert sand and gravel to uneven, muddy, and icy ground, giving the company a product that could, conceivably, be deployed just about anywhere tomorrow.
The company claims the new AFR can automatically mount modules on trackers every 40 seconds (3–5x faster than manual labour) with placement accuracy under +/-1mm. title: Scientists examine how nuclear device could be used to deflect asteroid threatening Earth
content: Researchers in the United States are developing three-dimensional simulations to examine how a nuclear device could be used to deflect or potentially disrupt an asteroid threatening Earth. The team from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) uses Spheral simulation code to more accurately model how an asteroid might respond when X-rays from a nuclear device detonated near its surface rapidly heat and vaporize material. After validating the approach against established asteroid-deflection models, researchers used Spheral to study three complex disruption scenarios. Hazardous asteroid impact could potentially be prevented The team revealed that unlike many natural disasters, a hazardous asteroid impact could potentially be prevented if the object is detected early enough. One approach is deflection — imparting a small change in velocity that causes the asteroid to miss Earth while largely remaining intact. Another approach is disruption, in which an asteroid is intentionally fragmented and dispersed so that no remaining piece poses a significant threat to the planet. NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test, or DART, demonstrated a kinetic-impact approach to deflection in 2022 by deliberately striking the asteroid moon Dimorphos. Nuclear mitigation represents an alternative emergency option, particularly for larger objects or scenarios with shorter warning times, because much more energy can be delivered to an asteroid than the kinetic energy of a spacecraft impactor, according to a press release. Two of the simulations showed strong signs of disruption, highlighting how high-fidelity 3D modeling can help researchers better understand how an asteroid could respond to a nuclear mitigation attempt, as per the release. “These simulations give us a much more detailed picture of how an asteroid may respond to a nuclear mitigation attempt,” said Isaiah Santistevan, who led the study. “Being able to model damage, fracture and material motion in three dimensions is an important step toward improving our ability to evaluate planetary defense options.” 1,500 one-dimensional Spheral simulations with asteroid deflection results Researchers revealed that to test the approach, they compared more than 1,500 one-dimensional Spheral simulations with asteroid deflection results from LLNL’s established Ares simulation code. The calculations showed close agreement between the two codes, giving researchers confidence to use Spheral for more complex 3D disruption simulations. Santistevan revealed that spheral is particularly well-suited to modeling problems involving material damage, fracture and fragmentation. The researchers then modeled three disruption scenarios involving an irregularly shaped asteroid roughly 160 meters across, varying both the distance of the hypothetical nuclear detonation and assumptions about how easily the asteroid material would fracture. In the longest-running simulation, about 98% of the asteroid material became fully damaged, meaning it had severely lost its ability to remain intact. The simulation also showed that roughly 97% was moving faster than the asteroid’s escape velocity, with the majority of material moving in opposite directions, further indicating that the body was breaking apart. “What’s encouraging is that we’re seeing the asteroid sustain extensive damage while material is also moving fast enough to escape its gravitational pull,” Santistevan said. “Those are important indicators that the asteroid is in the process of disrupting, and the 3D simulations allow us to examine that process in much greater detail.”

title: A single microwave line runs five silicon spin qubits with 99.9% accuracy
content: A quantum computer’s power depends not only on how many qubits it contains, but also on how accurately they can work together. Now, researchers have demonstrated a way to operate five silicon-based qubits simultaneously through a single microwave control line, maintaining operation accuracy at or above 99.9%. This approach could help make future quantum processors easier to scale without requiring a separate control line for every qubit. However, controlling several qubits at once is not as simple as sending them microwave signals together. Quantum computers need to perform operations in parallel to run error-correction routines, which help protect fragile quantum information. Yet the signals used to control one qubit can interfere with its neighbors, making their operations less accurate. In earlier experiments, this problem caused gate fidelity—a measure of how accurately a quantum operation is performed—to fall from 99.95% to around 99.5%. “Simultaneous control remains a major challenge in silicon devices, as fidelities typically degrade under parallel operation,” the researchers note in their study. Researchers from Japan’s RIKEN and collaborating institutions have now identified the main source of this interference and developed a way to compensate for it. The hidden frequency shift throwing qubits off course The team worked with five qubits made from electron spins trapped in tiny structures called quantum dots within a silicon/silicon-germanium device. “Silicon spin qubits, in particular, offer a promising path to scalable quantum computing due to their compatibility with industrial semiconductor manufacturing,” the researchers added. Microwave signals control these qubits, but a signal aimed at one can also affect its neighbors. This unwanted influence, known as crosstalk, can make quantum operations less accurate even when the neighboring qubits are not the intended targets. The researchers traced the main source of this interference to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift. A microwave signal can change a neighboring qubit’s effective energy levels, altering how its quantum state evolves. This produces an unwanted phase shift—a change in the relative timing of the waves that describe a quantum state—which can throw off the intended operation. A pair-by-pair fix keeps quantum operations accurate The team found that these phase shifts could be predicted by measuring how individual pairs of qubits affected one another. They used those measurements to compensate for the unwanted changes when several qubits operated together , avoiding the need to calibrate every possible combination separately. As study first author Yi-Hsien Wu explained, “Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts.” The results showed how effective the approach could be. When operated individually, the five qubits achieved gate fidelities above 99.99%, with the best approaching 99.999%. When up to three qubits operated simultaneously, their fidelities remained above 99.99%. Even when all five operated in parallel, their gate fidelities stayed at or above 99.9%. This level of accuracy meets a widely used benchmark for fault-tolerant quantum computing , where error-correction techniques help protect calculations from mistakes. It does not, however, mean the researchers have already built a fully fault-tolerant quantum computer. Faster quantum operations, with less power Using a shared microwave line could reduce the number of control connections needed by larger processors, saving space and potentially reducing the heat generated by control hardware. The researchers see the approach as a possible foundation for modules containing around ten qubits per shared line, although this larger configuration remains a future goal rather than a demonstrated result. Other challenges remain. Stronger microwave signals can speed up operations but also introduce unwanted disturbances that disrupt qubits’ delicate quantum states. The team proposes improving the tiny magnets used to control electron spins by integrating them into the chip’s wiring layers. These improved magnets could produce stronger local magnetic fields, potentially allowing faster operations at lower microwave power. For now, the achievement addresses one obstacle to scaling silicon quantum computers: maintaining accurate control when multiple qubits operate together. Extending the approach to larger arrays while controlling other sources of error will be essential before it can support practical, fault-tolerant quantum computing. The study is published in the journal Nature Physics .

title: Explained: How China’s ‘carrier killer’ missile threatens moving warships
content: Aircraft carriers allow navies to move air power across oceans without relying on nearby air bases. China developed the DF-21D missile to threaten the ships that make those operations possible. Known as a “carrier killer,” the DF-21D is a land-based anti-ship ballistic missile designed to strike large warships at sea. Its reputation comes from a combination of long range, a maneuverable reentry vehicle, and the challenge it presents to carrier defenses. The nickname, however, describes its intended mission. Whether it can successfully strike a moving carrier in wartime depends on much more than the missile itself. A ballistic missile built to attack ships The DF-21D belongs to China’s Dong Feng, or “East Wind,” missile family. Unlike variants intended to attack targets on land, it carries a conventional warhead for strikes against ships, including aircraft carriers. According to the Congressional Research Service , the missile has a range exceeding 1,500 kilometers (roughly 932 miles). That gives China a way to threaten naval vessels far from its coastline using land-based launchers. The distinction from an anti-ship cruise missile is important. Cruise missiles typically use powered flight within the atmosphere. A ballistic missile follows a high, arcing trajectory before its reentry vehicle descends toward the target. For naval planners, this introduces another direction and type of attack to defend against. CRS notes that before these weapons emerged, the US Navy had not faced highly accurate ballistic missiles capable of hitting moving ships at sea. A warhead that can adjust its approach Range alone cannot explain the “carrier killer” label. An aircraft carrier can change course and speed, making its position at launch different from its location when a missile arrives. The Pentagon’s 2024 China Military Power Report identifies a maneuverable reentry vehicle as a feature of the DF-21D. This vehicle carries the warhead back through the atmosphere and can adjust its flight path during the approach. That maneuverability supports the missile’s anti-ship role, although publicly available information does not establish its accuracy against a defended carrier under combat conditions. The DF-21D also operates from road-mobile launchers. These vehicles can relocate, making them harder to find and target than fixed launch sites. Mobility adds another complication for forces attempting to eliminate the threat before launch. Together, these features explain why the missile attracts attention: it combines a long-distance strike capability with a system intended to engage ships that do not remain stationary. Why sinking a carrier remains a difficult task A missile cannot attack a carrier effectively without reliable targeting information. China must first detect the ship, identify it, determine its position, and maintain sufficient tracking information to support the strike. That information must reach the launch unit, and the reentry vehicle must then find the intended ship. This sequence is commonly called the targeting “kill chain.” Failure at any stage can undermine the attack. Carrier groups also have defensive options. CRS discusses missile interceptors, electronic warfare, deception, and measures that obscure a ship’s location as ways to challenge anti-ship ballistic missiles. None guarantees protection, but their existence means the DF-21D’s range cannot be treated as an automatic no-go zone. The missile’s significance lies in the risk it introduces. A credible threat to a carrier can complicate decisions about positioning, protection, and how its aircraft conduct operations. That is why the “carrier killer” name has endured. The DF-21D was built to challenge a central instrument of American naval power, but its intended capability should not be confused with a guaranteed wartime outcome.

title: 7,300-year-old supervolcanic blast caused local population collapse in Japan
content: Around 7,300 years ago, one of Earth’s largest volcanic eruptions devastated prehistoric Japan, triggering severe population declines in certain regions while communities elsewhere continued to grow, according to new research. “This eruption must have been devastating,” said Peter Jordan, senior author and professor of archaeology at Lund University. Exploding from the seabed with little warning, “it battered the Japanese islands with powerful earthquakes and enormous tsunamis, and then blanketed the landscape with meters of volcanic ash,” he added. Lund University researchers found that the Kikai-Akahoya eruption produced markedly different demographic outcomes across Japan, challenging longstanding theories that the catastrophe had either wiped out entire communities or left them largely untouched. Until this latest study in Science Advances, two theories dominated academia: the eruption devastated southern Japan, causing widespread societal collapse, and some communities survived the catastrophe and maintained their traditions. Neither turned out to be true. Ancient communities faced different outcomes The eruption at the Kikai caldera occurred about 30 kilometers south of Kyushu, when Jomon hunter-gatherer communities inhabited Japan. The eruption registered a Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) of 7 and released an estimated 332 to 457 cubic kilometers of volcanic material. A Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) of 7 is classified as a super-colossal eruption. After analyzing 540 radiocarbon dates from archaeological sites across Japan, researchers used statistical models to reconstruct population trends before and after the catastrophe. Southern and central Kyushu experienced severe population declines. However, southern Kyushu’s population was already decreasing before the eruption, suggesting the disaster accelerated an existing trend. By contrast, populations along its northern coast continued growing despite the widespread environmental destruction. Researchers suggested that survivors from the south may have relocated northward, where coastal ecosystems recovered more quickly. “The disaster caused major loss of life. However, survivors migrated, forged new social relations, innovated new kinds of economy, and appear to have found creative ways to exist and later thrive in the new post-disaster conditions,” said lead author Enrico Crema, a professor at Cambridge University. Population declines extended beyond the eruption zone The explosion also affected demographic regions farther from the volcano . Some communities stagnated or declined afterward, including areas along Japan’s Pacific coast. Researchers presented several hypotheses: damage to food resources from volcanic ash , climate change, and adverse health effects on humans and animals. However, the researchers acknowledged that the available evidence could not conclusively establish which environmental factors caused the population changes. Even so, the findings challenged traditional interpretations of the eruption as an event that permanently devastated prehistoric Japan through widespread societal collapse. Instead, the researchers found traces of regional population losses, continued growth, and possible migration between affected communities. Society did not collapse after the volcanic explosion , although the region was heavily affected. The study provided researchers with “a deeper understanding of the contingent ways in which cultures and societies cope with sudden shocks and catastrophes,” said Jordan. “Even in the most impossible situations, survivors and communities have choices, however limited: they need to act and make decisions; they need to adjust, collaborate, and find new connections and social networks,” Jordan concluded .

title: From Nimitz-class ships to Gerald R. Ford: A complete look at US aircraft carriers
content: The United States has 11 commissioned aircraft carriers as of October 2026. The fleet includes 10 Nimitz-class ships and one Gerald R. Ford-class carrier, all powered by nuclear reactors. However, the number comes with an important qualification. Having 11 commissioned carriers does not mean the Navy can send all 11 into combat simultaneously. Some undergo maintenance or lengthy overhauls, while others conduct training or prepare for deployment. The count also excludes amphibious assault ships and carriers that have yet to enter commissioned service. Those distinctions matter as the Navy prepares to retire its oldest carrier and bring its next ship into the fleet. Which aircraft carriers does the US have? The Nimitz class accounts for most of the American carrier fleet. Its ten ships are USS Nimitz, USS Dwight D. Eisenhower, USS Carl Vinson, USS Theodore Roosevelt, USS Abraham Lincoln, USS George Washington , USS John C. Stennis, USS Harry S. Truman, USS Ronald Reagan, and USS George H.W. Bush. Their hull numbers run consecutively from CVN-68 through CVN-77. The designation CVN identifies a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. The eleventh ship, USS Gerald R. Ford, is designated CVN-78. Commissioned in July 2017, it introduced the next generation of American aircraft carriers. Ford uses electromagnetic catapults to launch aircraft, replacing the steam-powered catapults aboard Nimitz-class ships. Its design also incorporates new aircraft recovery equipment and weapons elevators. Together, these carriers provide mobile airfields that allow the Navy to conduct aviation operations at sea. Their embarked aircraft perform missions ranging from strike operations and air defense to surveillance and electronic warfare. Nuclear propulsion gives the ships considerable endurance, but it does not eliminate their supply requirements. Aircraft fuel, food, ammunition, and other supplies still need replenishment. Why all 11 cannot be deployed together A commissioned carrier remains part of the fleet even when maintenance prevents it from deploying. Consequently, the inventory total provides only part of the picture of American naval aviation capacity. Carriers move through deployment, maintenance, and training periods. Major shipyard work can remove a vessel from operational availability for years without removing it from the commissioned fleet. USS Harry S. Truman provides a current example. The ship departed Norfolk for Newport News Shipbuilding on September 30, 2026, to begin the shipyard phase of its refueling and complex overhaul. According to the Navy’s announcement , the work includes reactor refueling and extensive modernization, with completion scheduled for November 2031. Another source of confusion is the Navy’s amphibious assault fleet. These ships have large flight decks and can operate helicopters, tiltrotors, and short-takeoff and vertical-landing aircraft. However, their primary role centers on supporting Marine expeditionary operations. The Navy classifies them separately as amphibious assault ships, designated LHA or LHD, rather than including them in its 11-carrier CVN fleet. Will the carrier count change soon? The transition between USS Nimitz and the future USS John F. Kennedy makes the date attached to any carrier count particularly important. Nimitz, commissioned in May 1975, remains included in the fleet. Although earlier plans anticipated retirement in 2026, its service was extended into 2027. Meanwhile, John F. Kennedy, designated CVN-79, has not yet joined the commissioned carrier fleet. The Navy announced its preliminary acceptance on September 29, 2026, with formal delivery scheduled for spring 2027. That milestone permits additional at-sea testing and crew training while the shipbuilder completes remaining systems testing. It does not mean the carrier has been commissioned or is ready for deployment. For now, the answer remains 11 commissioned carriers. How many are available for operations is a separate question, shaped by maintenance schedules, training requirements, and the transition between retiring ships and their replacements.

title: S-400 vs S-500: What is the difference between Russia’s air-defense systems?
content: Russia’s S-400 and S-500 are both mobile, ground-based air-defense systems designed to intercept threats at long distances. But they are intended to do different jobs within Russia’s broader air- and missile-defense network. The S-400 is a mature system built primarily to engage aircraft, cruise missiles, and some ballistic-missile threats. The newer S-500 is designed to extend those capabilities, with a stronger emphasis on intercepting advanced ballistic missiles and potentially targets operating near the edge of space. The biggest distinction is not simply range. It is the type of threat each system is designed to counter, the interceptors and radars it uses, and how much of its advertised capability can be independently verified. S-400: Russia’s established long-range air defense The S-400 Triumf, known by NATO as the SA-21 Growler , entered service in 2007. It is designed to engage a range of aerial threats, including aircraft, drones, and cruise missiles, while also providing a limited capability against ballistic missiles. The system uses different interceptor missiles for different targets, rather than relying on one missile for every engagement. The S-400’s advertised maximum engagement range depends on the missile used. The 40N6 family is associated with ranges of up to 400 kilometers (about 249 miles), while other interceptors have shorter ranges and different engagement envelopes. That figure should not be confused with the distance at which the system can reliably detect or engage every target: radar coverage, target altitude, and the target’s characteristics all matter. The S-400’s main role is therefore broad-area air defense. It can threaten aircraft and other aerial targets across a large area, while offering a more limited layer of protection against ballistic missiles. It is not, however, a dedicated substitute for every specialized strategic missile-defense system . S-500: A higher layer for missile defense The S-500 Prometheus is intended to add a more specialized layer to Russia’s defenses. Its planned capabilities include intercepting ballistic missiles and, according to Russian claims, certain hypersonic weapons and targets in low Earth orbit. The system is associated with the 77N6 interceptor family for ballistic-missile defense and the 40N6M for aircraft and cruise-missile targets. The latter reflects some overlap with the S-400, rather than a completely separate set of capabilities. Open-source estimates put the S-500’s maximum interceptor range at roughly 500-600 kilometers (310-373 miles), but these figures are not equivalent to a verified engagement range against every type of target. Its radar suite also combines general air surveillance with specialized tracking and engagement of ballistic threats. Claims that the S-500 can intercept hypersonic weapons or satellites deserve particular caution. Publicly available information does not independently establish the full performance of these capabilities, and details about the system’s most specialized interceptors remain limited. How do the two systems differ in practice? The S-400 is the more established and widely deployed system, designed to serve a major part of Russia’s long-range air-defense network. The S-500 is a more specialized addition, intended to strengthen defenses against demanding ballistic-missile threats and potentially targets at near-space altitudes. Their roles overlap, but the S-500 is not simply an S-400 with a longer-range missile. It uses a different combination of radars and interceptors to address threats that require more specialized tracking and interception. In principle, the two systems can complement each other: the S-400 handles a broad range of aerial threats, while the S-500 adds a higher layer of missile defense. Russia announced in December 2025 that its first S-500-equipped regiment had entered combat duty. However, officials disclosed few operational details, and public information about the system’s numbers, deployment configuration, and demonstrated performance remains limited.

title: Ukrainian drones strike fuel depots and tech hubs near Russia’s St. Petersburg: Reports
content: Ukrainian drone strikes hit multiple infrastructure sites in St. Petersburg and Russia’s surrounding Leningrad region early on October 18, setting fires at an oil terminal and fuel depot, damaging a data center operated by technology company VK, and disrupting electricity supplies to about 20,000 residents. The reported targets also included an Ozon e-commerce logistics hub and a bridge on the city’s Western High-Speed Diameter. Russian officials confirmed an overnight drone attack and damage to infrastructure, while open-source investigators reported fires at several locations. The strikes follow other reported Ukrainian attacks on Russian technology infrastructure earlier in October, including incidents involving Yandex data centers in the Vladimir, Ryazan and Kaluga regions, as well as a reported strike on a Sberbank data center facility in the Saratov region. Oil infrastructure and fuel distribution hit St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the city had come under attack by UAVs , with fires reported across four districts. He acknowledged damage at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, a major petroleum transshipment facility serving Russia’s Baltic region. Open-source analysis by independent Russian outlet Astra also identified a fire at the terminal and a separate blaze at the Ruchyi oil depot in the city’s Krasnogvardeisky district. The depot has a reported storage capacity of 3,900 cubic meters, equivalent to approximately 137,400 cubic feet, and handles AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline as well as commercial diesel, the Kyiv Post reported . The reported damage could affect facilities involved in storing and moving fuel, although the extent of operational disruption at either site was not immediately clear. The petroleum terminal’s role in regional fuel logistics makes it a significant infrastructure site, but the available reports did not establish how much storage or handling capacity was lost. Astra also reported that municipal emergency alerts failed to warn residents in advance, with notifications arriving after impacts or being substantially delayed. The claim also shows a separate concern surrounding overnight attacks and whether local warning systems can provide timely information to people in affected areas. Drone strikes disrupt digital and power infrastructure The attack also extended into the Leningrad region, where drones reportedly hit a data center operated by VK, the Russian technology group behind the VKontakte social network and other online services. The facility is located in Novosergievka, in the Vsevolozhsk district. VK representatives said their services continued operating normally, but users across Russia reported connection problems and outages affecting VKontakte and parts of its wider platform. Astra’s investigators reported that an electrical substation next to the data center was also damaged. Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed damage to electrical distribution infrastructure and emergency power cuts that left approximately 20,000 residents without electricity. The available reports did not establish whether the reported online disruptions resulted directly from damage to the data center, the nearby substation, or other effects of the attack. Russian e-commerce company Ozon separately confirmed that an aerial impact caused a fire at its fulfillment center on Sofiyskaya Street in St. Petersburg’s Kolpino district. The facility covers approximately 850,000 square feet and is one of the company’s major logistics sites in northwestern Russia.

title: 10 fastest US military aircraft and the engineering behind their speed
content: The fastest aircraft flown by the US military include fighters, reconnaissance jets, and experimental rocket planes. Some entered service and flew missions for decades, while others made only a small number of test flights to explore the limits of speed and altitude.Their designs reflect the different reasons for flying fast, from intercepting enemy bombers to gathering intelligence over defended territory. Reaching those speeds required powerful engines, specialized airframes, and materials capable of withstanding intense heat.This list ranks 10 of the fastest crewed aircraft flown in US military service or military flight-test programs, including joint research efforts. 1. North American X-15 — 4,520 mphWikimedia CommonsAccording to NASA, Air Force pilot William “Pete” Knight reached 4,520 mph in the X-15A-2 on October 3, 1967. The joint NASA–Air Force–Navy program investigated hypersonic flight, placing this rocket-powered research aircraft well ahead of every other entry here. A modified B-52 carried the X-15 to launch altitude before its rocket engine took over, and the aircraft later returned for an unpowered landing. For the fastest flight, external propellant tanks extended engine operation, while an ablative coating protected the aircraft against intense aerodynamic heating.2. Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird — 2,193 mphThe SR-71 turned sustained high-speed flight into an operational reconnaissance capability. On July 28, 1976, a Blackbird established an absolute speed record for its class of approximately 2,193 mph, securing its place among aviation’s most remarkable aircraft.Its Pratt & Whitney J58 engines were designed to operate above 80,000 feet at speeds exceeding three times the speed of sound. That performance supported the Blackbird’s reconnaissance mission, allowing it to survey vast areas from high altitude while traveling faster than conventional fighters.3. Bell X-2 Starbuster — 2,094 mphAir Force Captain Milburn “Mel” Apt flew the X-2 to 2,094 mph on September 27, 1956, becoming the first person to exceed three times the speed of sound. The rocket-powered research aircraft investigated aerodynamic heating and control at speeds beyond those explored by the earlier X-1 series.Stainless steel and a copper-nickel alloy helped its structure withstand the demanding flight conditions. However, a turn after the speed run triggered an uncontrollable tumble, and Apt died after separating the aircraft’s escape capsule.4. Lockheed YF-12A — 2,070 mphThe YF-12A explored whether Lockheed’s high-speed reconnaissance aircraft technology could become a long-range interceptor.During Air Force testing on May 1, 1965, it established an official record of approximately 2,070 mph 2,070 mph.Its largely titanium structure helped withstand the temperatures generated during sustained high-speed flight. Although it never entered operational military service, the YF-12 later supported joint Air Force–NASA investigations into aerodynamic heating, propulsion, and structural behavior.5. North American XB-70 Valkyrie — 2,056 mphWikimedia CommonsThe enormous XB-70 Valkyrie was conceived as a nuclear-armed bomber capable of flying higher and faster than the B-52. The National Museum of the US Air Force lists its maximum speed as 2,056 mph at 73,000 feet, powered by six afterburning engines.Its outer wingtips folded downward during supersonic flight, helping reduce drag and improve directional stability. The planned operational bomber never materialized, but the experimental aircraft supplied research data on the challenges of flying a large aircraft at such speeds.6. McDonnell Douglas F-15 Eagle — 1,875 mphThe F-15 brought extreme performance into an operational air-superiority fighter, with the US Air Force publishing a maximum speed of 1,875 mph. Its design combined powerful engines with relatively low wing loading to deliver strong acceleration and maneuverability. That combination made the Eagle more than an aircraft built for a straight-line sprint. High thrust relative to its weight helped it accelerate while climbing, giving pilots performance they could use during an engagement rather than only during a maximum-speed run.7. Bell X-1A — approximately 1,650 mphChuck Yeager pushed the rocket-powered X-1A to approximately 1,650 mph on December 12, 1953. The Air Force test flight extended the work begun by the original X-1, taking piloted aircraft deeper into supersonic flight.Reaching that speed was only part of the challenge, as the aircraft subsequently tumbled out of control. Yeager recovered, but the flight exposed dangerous handling problems that engineers needed to understand before aircraft could safely operate at still higher speeds.8. General Dynamics F-111 Aardvark — 1,650 mphThe F-111 combined a published high-altitude maximum of approximately 1,650 mph with a mission centered on attacking ground targets, matching the X-1A’s rounded figure. That headline speed described its high-altitude performance, rather than the speed used while following terrain close to the ground.Its movable wings allowed different configurations for takeoff, landing, and fast flight, while terrain-following radar supported low-altitude penetration. Despite its fighter designation, the Aardvark became a strike aircraft whose usefulness depended on reaching targets in difficult conditions as much as outright speed.9. McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II — 1,606 mphThe F-4 Phantom II earned its place through a record flight rather than a routine combat configuration. A specially modified Phantom reached approximately 1,606 mph during Operation Skyburner in November 1961, demonstrating the performance available from its twin-engine design.The aircraft subsequently handled air combat, ground attack, reconnaissance, and the suppression of enemy air defenses.Its speed record should therefore be read as a test achievement, rather than a claim that every operational Phantom could reach the same figure while carrying weapons.10. Convair F-106A Delta Dart — 1,525 mphWikimedia CommonsThe Convair F-106A Delta Dart was an all-weather interceptor built to defend against attacking enemy aircraft. It entered US Air Force service in 1959 and had a maximum speed of 1,525 mph, powered by a single Pratt & Whitney J75 afterburning turbojet.Its Hughes MA-1 guidance and fire-control system could direct the aircraft into an attack position and launch its missiles. The system could then guide the interceptor back toward its base, with the pilot taking control for landing.ConclusionFrom operational fighters to rocket-powered research planes, these aircraft pushed the limits of US military aviation.Their speed supported missions ranging from intercepting threats to gathering intelligence and exploring flight conditions no pilot had previously experienced.Reaching those speeds required more than powerful engines, as engineers also had to overcome intense heat and dangerous control problems. Some designs entered frontline service, while others remained experimental, but both helped expand the understanding of high-speed flight.

title: Black hole spotted tearing apart a star 3,500 light-years off-center
content: Can a dying star reveal the location of a black hole that has otherwise gone unnoticed? Turns out, it can.Astronomers have now traced a stellar destruction event to a massive black hole about 3,500 light-years from the center of its host galaxy. This discovery offers a rare look at a so-called wandering black hole and raises a further question: how did it end up so far from home?Most massive black holes are found at the centers of galaxies, where they can sometimes reveal themselves by pulling in surrounding matter. However, black holes away from galactic centers can remain nearly invisible when they are not actively feeding. The newly studied event, called TDE 2023mfm, shows how a star’s destruction can expose one of these otherwise elusive objects. “We present the discovery and analysis of the optically selected tidal disruption event (TDE) 2023mfm, which originates from a wandering massive black hole (MBH) in a massive galaxy,” the study authors note.Catching a wandering black holeThe event began when a star ventured too close to a massive black hole and was pulled apart by its intense gravity. This phenomenon, known as a tidal disruption event (TDE), sends stellar debris around the black hole and can produce a bright flare that astronomers detect across different wavelengths.The Zwicky Transient Facility first spotted TDE 2023mfm on June 28, 2023. The researchers subsequently examined observations from several observatories, including the Hubble Space Telescope, Swift, Keck, Lick, Chandra, XMM-Newton, and the Very Large Array (VLA).Each instrument offered a different clue. Optical and ultraviolet observations tracked the flare’s brightness and temperature, while optical spectroscopy helped identify the type of event. The researchers found a broad hydrogen emission line, a signature consistent with a category known as TDE-H. The flare also remained blue and hot, reaching a temperature of around 22,000 Kelvin for more than a month after its peak.The light curve (the record of how an object’s brightness changes over time) showed that the event rose to its peak and then gradually faded. It remained above half its peak brightness for nearly 48 days, closely matching the duration and peak brightness of another off-center event, TDE 2024tvd.Crucially, high-resolution optical, ultraviolet, and radio observations placed the flare about 1.08 kiloparsecs, or roughly 3,500 light-years, from the galaxy’s center. The team estimated that the black hole responsible has a mass of roughly one million to 10 million times that of the Sun, although the precise value depends on the method used.The researchers found no X-ray emission clearly attributable to the disruption. Although a faint X-ray source was present, it most likely came from the galaxy’s nucleus. That absence did not rule out a TDE: some such events remain X-ray faint even years after a star is destroyed, as seen in other unusual black hole feeding events.A delayed radio signal deepens the mysteryThe black hole’s location is clear, but its history is not. One possibility is that it arrived with a smaller galaxy that merged with its host. The researchers identified a faint stellar population at the same location, with an estimated mass of around 10 million to 100 million Suns. If this population is the remnant of a smaller galaxy, much of that galaxy’s original stellar material may have been stripped away.Other proposed explanations involve black holes being flung away from galactic centers by gravitational interactions or gravitational-wave recoil following a merger. However, the host galaxy still contains a black hole at its own center, identified through a faint active galactic nucleus. This makes a minor merger a plausible explanation, but the observations do not establish how the wandering black hole arrived there.“The radio emission, on the other hand, tells a different story,” the researchers said.Unlike some comparable TDEs, this event produced no detected radio emission early on. A faint signal emerged only about 991 days after the optical discovery, roughly 2.7 years later, and evolved slowly. This late signal may come from an outflow of material launched by the disruption, but the observations cannot yet establish its origin. Differences in the surrounding gas or the angle from which the event is viewed could also explain the unusual behavior.The findings show how combining observations across the electromagnetic spectrum can uncover black holes that ordinary searches might miss. The team says further high-resolution radio observations, particularly with very long baseline interferometry, could help determine the source’s size and clarify the nature of the outflow. Moreover, finding additional off-center black holes could help astronomers understand how galaxies merge and how their central black holes evolve.The study is published on the arXiv.

title: China's space rice experiment could help astronauts grow their own food
content: Chinese astronauts aboard the Tiangong space station have completed what they called the “Autumn harvest” of their in-space rice cultivation experiment. According to reports, the astronauts successfully collected, sowed, and stored a new batch of rice on the space station.Reported on October 18, this marks a major milestone in the project’s hopes to reproduce rice over successive generations entirely in space. The first generation of rice involved the use of seeds brought from Earth and sown in orbit. These have been allowed to germinate, mature, flower, and seed in microgravity.Seeds harvested from these plants are then being used to grow a second generation entirely in orbit. This is crucial, as the new plants will develop from seeds produced in microgravity rather than on EarthRice in spaceAccording to the Chinese Academy of Sciences, this experiment began earlier in 2026 and is intended to complete two seed-to-seed cycles. This is not the first time rice has been grown on the space station (in fact, this was achieved back in 2022).The seeds produced by those plants were returned to Earth, where researchers successfully grew another three generations. But what is interesting here is that the astronauts are investigating the genetic stability of rice plants in microgravity.Living organisms on Earth have evolved under Earth’s gravity, so removing that might, in theory, influence how the plants develop and reproduce, grow, and mature. They are particularly interested in not only genetic changes, but also things like epigenetics (or how genes express themselves). They also want to see how rice adapts over successive generations in space. Ultimately, they want to see if foodstuffs like rice will develop over successive generations of growing in space.Interestingly, researchers are also comparing ordinary Earth-grown seeds with descendants of rice previously grown in space in 2022. This should help them determine whether previous exposure to microgravity leaves any lasting effects that influence how subsequent generations develop.Additionally, the team is also investigating two methods of crop growth in space to see which, if any, is more valuable under microgravity conditions. The first is sexual reproduction, as we’ve already mentioned above.Part of the puzzle, not a solutionThe second is something called asexual regrowth (called ratooning). This method involves harvesting the rice while maintaining the parent plant’s root systems. This will allow the plant to grow new shoots and ultimately produce more rice. This method could be more valuable as it bypasses the need to replant crops. If the same plants can produce multiple harvests of rice, rather than just one, that would be far more efficient in the long run.Whichever method (or a combination of both) is best is yet to be seen, but the ultimate ambition is to find a way to produce food in space to reduce the need for resupply from Earth. Critically, this kind of experiment doesn’t necessarily mean we can then transfer the technology to places like Mars or the Moon.There is a huge difference between the conditions on a space station and the conditions on another celestial body. It is an important part of such a puzzle, but will likely not yield the solution.

title: US military seeks expanded island missile network to counter China
content: Senior US Army leaders have highlighted the importance of having more land-based troops and assets in the Indo-Pacific should a conflict erupt in the region. In fact, this would likely be as important as Navy and Air Force resources in the region.During the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting this week, General Ron Clark (Commander of the US Army Pacific) explained that “the tyranny of distance” would be a major factor during such a conflict. That might sound a little strange on the surface (no pun intended). The Pacific is an enormous ocean, so logically, emphasis should be placed on naval and associated air assets.But that is not necessarily the case. In fact, islands, regional allies, and other land-based assets, like missile systems, could be just as important. Arguably more in some circumstances. Gen. Clark’s comments are essentially saying that, should such a conflict erupt, the US would be at a major disadvantage from the outset. China would be conducting such a war effectively in its backyard, with supply chains much closer to home. Air, land, and sea forces as oneThe US, on the other hand, would need to project and supply its power thousands of miles away. Ships and aircraft need fuel and ammunition, maintenance, and other logistical support.That would not be an easy task over such distances. Chinese assets, on the other hand, would benefit from support and a supply chain very close to potential hotspots like Taiwan.So, what can be done about it? Well, various island chains are conveniently placed in the region and could be put to use to even the odds. Allied nations like Japan and the Philippines also happen to be dotted around the Indo-Pacific. This is called the “Island Chain Strategy.”These islands and allied nations could be used to seed mobile missile launchers, radar systems, and air defenses on friendly soil. Such assets, it is argued, could be used for critical things like anti-ship warfare, air defense, and long-range strikes. They could also be used as vital hubs and caches to support US asset logistics. Mobile missile systems in particular would be of great importance, since they are harder to locate and neutralize by the enemy. Interestingly, this is not just theoretical either. The US has already tested this back in May 2026 in the Philippines when they test-fired a Tomahawk missile from one of its stationed Typhon systems.Eroding China’s “home” advantageAll of this ultimately comes down to deterrence. Or, in other words, make any action by China so potentially dangerous that they’d think twice about doing so. Take Taiwan, for example. If the US can position sufficient military assets in nearby allied territories, it could significantly increase the potential costs of a Chinese invasion, despite China’s geographical advantage.Sounds good in theory, but there would also be a catch. Land-based assets, even if located on island chains, are not invulnerable. China, for its part, has substantial ballistic and cruise missile stockpiles of its own that can threaten these bases in kind.What’s more, the problem they are trying to solve is also hampered by the same “tyranny of distance” in not being immune to the need for supply and support. But, that said, what is clear is that land-based forces and weapons systems can help balance the odds for naval and air assets hundreds or even thousands of miles away.To this end, the “clear” boundaries between the different services are increasingly becoming blurred.

title: US nuclear fusion reactor to test custom exhaust to tame plasma heat
content: Scientists developing nuclear fusion have launched a new initiative to solve one of the most stubborn engineering puzzles standing between experimental reactors and commercial electricity.The DIII-D National Fusion Facility in California is teaming up with Japanese engineering firm Kyoto Fusioneering. Together, they will build and test a specialised exhaust system designed to handle the ferocious heat produced inside a fusion reactor. The system will be installed directly into DIII-D’s tokamak, a testbed device funded by the US Department of Energy.Nuclear fusion generates clean power by fusing light atoms together, the same process that fuels the sun. Most research takes place inside donut-shaped magnetic chambers known as tokamaks. However, containing matter heated to over 100 million degrees Celsius poses a serious risk to machine walls.A new operational approach for tokamaksStandard reactors suffer from intense, sudden heat pulses that can erode interior surfaces over time. To overcome this, researchers are turning to a design known as “negative triangularity.”“Negative triangularity, or plasma in a reverse ‘D’ shape, is a potentially transformative operational approach for tokamaks, donut-shaped fusion devices that contain plasma with magnetic fields,” explained Kyoto Fusioneering.This alternative geometry offers an elegant physical advantage. It dampens unstable heat bursts and radiates excess thermal energy away smoothly before it can strike reactor walls. Yet despite its promise, nobody has tested the configuration with an industrial-grade exhaust system capable of handling its unique particle flows.Constructing purpose-built ‘divertor’The new venture directly targets that blind spot. Kyoto Fusioneering will manufacture heat-resistant tiles to construct a purpose-built “divertor,” the component acting as the reactor’s chimney. Once installed, researchers from DIII-D, Kyoto Fusioneering, and Columbia University will fire up the tokamak for extensive trials.“Our need to understand negative triangularity in a commercially relevant device setup led to the collaboration,” said Suk-Ho Hong, DIII-D Fusion Technology Outreach Coordinator. He noted that the project will allow scientists to evaluate the approach on an active, cost-effective test platform.Engineers face a delicate balancing act inside the chamber. The machine must sustain a blazing core hot enough for fusion to occur, while the outer edge must remain cool enough not to melt surrounding equipment. Trials will test how well the reverse-D plasma behaves during extended operations, measuring heat loads and mechanical strain on internal components.To refine future reactor designs“High neutron loads and heat fluxes are among the most critical challenges to the viability of fusion power plants,” concluded Bibake Uppal, President of Kyoto Fusioneering America. He emphasized that testing novel divertor concepts is vital to proving commercial viability.The findings will feed into broader roadmaps set by the US Department of Energy. Test results will help physicists validate whole-plant computer models, evaluate plasma stability, and refine materials needed for future pilot plants.Experimental data will be shared freely across the international DIII-D user network. By opening up the research, the partnership aims to help commercial fusion ventures worldwide design reactors capable of supplying steady power to the grid.

title: How hypersonic missiles survive extreme heat at speeds above Mach 5
content: Hypersonic missiles can race through the atmosphere at more than five times the speed of sound, exposing their surfaces to temperatures hot enough to damage or destroy conventional aircraft materials. Their survival depends on a combination of heat-resistant materials, protective coatings, carefully engineered shapes, and, in some designs, systems that actively remove heat.The challenge is not simply moving fast. At hypersonic speeds, air cannot move out of the vehicle’s way quickly enough, creating strong shock waves and compressing the surrounding gas. This process heats the air around the missile, while aerodynamic heating transfers energy to its surface. The nose and leading edges often face the most intense thermal loads.NASA says thermal protection systems are designed to keep this heat from reaching internal structures and components. For hypersonic weapons, that means engineering a vehicle that can survive both extreme temperatures and the mechanical stresses of high-speed flight.1. Heat-resistant materials form the first line of defenseOrdinary aircraft materials, including many conventional metal alloys, can lose strength at the temperatures encountered during hypersonic flight. Engineers therefore turn to specialized composites and ceramics.One important option is carbon-carbon composite, made from carbon fibers embedded in a carbon matrix. It can withstand extremely high temperatures while retaining useful structural properties, making it valuable for exposed surfaces such as nose tips and leading edges.However, carbon-carbon has a weakness. Oxygen can attack the material at high temperatures. Protective coatings are therefore essential to limit oxidation and prevent the structure from degrading.Ceramic matrix composites offer another option. Materials such as silicon-carbide-reinforced composites combine high-temperature resistance with relatively low weight. Researchers are also studying ultra-high-temperature ceramics for components exposed to especially severe heating.DARPA’s hypersonics materials research highlights the difficulty of protecting sharp leading edges, where thermal loads are particularly intense. A material must survive the heat without losing the shape needed for aerodynamic performance.2. Sometimes, the missile is designed to burn awayNot every hypersonic vehicle needs to survive repeated flights. Some can use ablative thermal protection, in which the outer material gradually decomposes, chars, melts, or erodes, carrying heat away from the underlying structure.Think of it as a sacrificial shield. Instead of preventing all damage to the surface, the system uses controlled material loss to protect what lies beneath. NASA has used ablative heat shields for spacecraft returning through Earth’s atmosphere, where the thermal environment can be particularly severe. Similar principles can help protect expendable high-speed vehicles.The trade-off is that ablative protection changes the surface as it works. That can make it unsuitable for vehicles that must preserve their aerodynamic shape over repeated missions.3. Active cooling can remove heat before it builds upSome advanced designs explore active cooling, in which a fluid circulates through channels within a structure to carry heat away from vulnerable areas. Fuel can potentially serve as a coolant before it enters an engine, absorbing heat as it passes through specially designed passages. Other concepts combine active cooling with insulating layers, allowing the outer surface to withstand high temperatures while limiting heat transfer into the vehicle.A 2026 study published in Applied Thermal Engineering examined a combined thermal-protection structure using ceramic insulation and cooling channels. Its simulations found that cooling with aviation kerosene could improve the modeled system’s thermal-protection efficiency. These are research results, not proof that the same arrangement is used in operational missiles.4. Shape and flight time matter, tooMaterials alone cannot solve the problem. Missile designers must balance aerodynamic efficiency against heat management. Sharp edges can improve aerodynamic performance in some flight regimes, but they also concentrate heat. Blunter shapes can spread heating over a larger area, though they may increase drag. Engineers must also account for how long a vehicle remains in a dense atmosphere, its flight path, and how heat distributes across its surface.Boost-glide vehicles, such as the US Army’s planned Dark Eagle, use a rocket to accelerate a glide vehicle before it enters the atmosphere. Hypersonic cruise missiles, by contrast, are designed to sustain powered flight at hypersonic speeds, potentially using an air-breathing scramjet engine. Their thermal challenges overlap, but their propulsion systems and flight profiles differ.The bottom line is that no single miracle material makes a missile heatproof. Surviving Mach 5 and beyond requires an integrated system of materials, coatings, cooling, structural design, and flight planning.

title: Rocket or scramjet? The technology behind hypersonic missile propulsion
content: Hypersonic weapons promise to reach targets at more than five times the speed of sound, but getting them there requires some serious engineering. Two propulsion technologies play central roles: conventional rockets, which carry their own oxygen supply, and scramjets, which breathe air from the atmosphere.Neither is universally better. Rockets provide the acceleration needed to reach hypersonic speeds, while scramjets can sustain powered flight through the atmosphere without carrying an onboard oxidizer. In some hypersonic weapons, the two technologies work together.Rockets provide the initial boostRocket engines carry both fuel and an oxidizer, so that they can generate thrust without atmospheric oxygen. This makes them versatile: they can operate from a standstill, at high altitudes, and even in space.For hypersonic weapons, that capability is particularly valuable during acceleration. A rocket can rapidly propel a vehicle to the speeds needed for its mission, whether it is carrying a conventional payload or releasing a glide vehicle that continues toward its target without sustained engine power.The drawback is that rockets must carry their oxidizer alongside their fuel. That adds mass, which could otherwise be allocated to fuel, payload, or other components. Sustaining powered flight can also consume propellant quickly, depending on the vehicle’s design and flight profile.Rockets remain an established technology with decades of operational experience behind them. For boost-glide weapons and missiles that need powerful initial acceleration, they are a natural choice.Scramjets use air to sustain hypersonic flightA scramjet, short for supersonic combustion ramjet, takes a different approach. It draws oxygen from the atmosphere rather than carrying its own oxidizer. As the vehicle moves forward at high speed, its inlet compresses incoming air before fuel is injected and burned.The key distinction is that airflow through the combustion chamber remains supersonic. This allows the engine to operate at hypersonic flight speeds without the rotating compressor and turbine found in conventional jet engines.Scramjets can potentially sustain hypersonic cruise more efficiently than a rocket because they do not need to carry an onboard oxygen supply. But they usually cannot generate enough thrust from a standstill to accelerate into their operating range. A booster or another propulsion system must first accelerate the vehicle to a sufficient speed.Keeping combustion stable in airflow moving at several times the speed of sound is also exceptionally difficult. The engine must manage fuel mixing, pressure, and extreme temperatures in milliseconds.NASA and DARPA demonstrated the technologyNASA’s X-43A experimental aircraft helped establish that scramjet propulsion could work in free flight. In November 2004, the research vehicle reached approximately Mach 9.6 after a rocket booster accelerated it to the required speed and altitude. Its scramjet operated briefly before the vehicle completed its test flight.Military research has followed a similar path. In 2021, DARPA and the US Air Force announced a successful flight test of the Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept (HAWC), a scramjet-powered cruise missile demonstrator developed by Raytheon. A 2023 HAWC flight demonstrated another design developed by Lockheed Martin.These tests showed that air-breathing hypersonic propulsion is feasible, but turning experimental systems into reliable, affordable weapons remains a substantial engineering challenge.Why hypersonic weapons may need bothRockets and scramjets solve different problems. Rockets offer powerful acceleration and greater flexibility across operating environments. Scramjets offer the potential for sustained, powered hypersonic flight within the atmosphere without carrying an oxidizer.That is why some proposed hypersonic cruise missiles combine the technologies. A rocket booster accelerates the vehicle, then separates once the scramjet can take over. Boost-glide weapons follow a different approach, using rocket propulsion to accelerate a vehicle that then glides toward its target.Ultimately, the better technology depends on the mission. Rockets remain the more versatile propulsion option, while scramjets are promising for sustained atmospheric hypersonic cruise. Neither eliminates the heat, control, cost, and reliability challenges that make hypersonic weapons so difficult to develop.

title: Finetuning layers in electronics could boost devices' performance
content: Researchers have found that finetuning composition of microscopic layers could yield major performance improvements in devices. The University of Ottawa team revealed that small changes to the materials and structure of the electronic devices dramatically improve their efficiency and sustainability.Because these devices rely on carefully arranged layers to conduct electricity, adjusting their composition at the microscopic level may be key in creating electronics that use less power and support more sustainable designs. By changing these layers, researchers hope to vastly improve the function of devices — particularly smaller, wearable, and biodegradable ones.Improvements can even open new uses for electronicsBenoit Lessard’s research group at the University of Ottawa is exploring different materials that can serve as the base layer for these conducting stacks, known as thin-film transistors.“It’s really important to keep in mind the bottom layer when you put the next layer on top, because it’s going to influence how that next layer organizes, how those molecules line up,” said Lessard.The team highlighted that the improvements can even open new uses for electronics, such as reducing harm from street drugs. Lessard’s group is developing sensors that can use electrochemical reactions to determine not just which substances are present in a sample, but the quantity of each.Current tests for drugs like fentanyl are “useful for telling you a yes or no,” Lessard said. But knowing exactly how much fentanyl is present in a sample would be extremely helpful both for drug users and the healthcare workers treating them.Electronic devices often depend on thin-film transistorsElectronic devices often depend on thin-film transistors, which control the movement of electrical signals and are widely used in display technologies and other electronic applications. Their performance depends not only on the materials used but also on how these materials are arranged at the molecular level.The layer beneath the active material plays a particularly important role. Its chemical composition and physical properties can influence how molecules in the upper layer align and organise themselves. Even small changes in this arrangement can affect how efficiently electrical charges move through a device and how much voltage is needed for it to function.Researchers investigated n-type Organic thin-film transistors (OTFTs) based on bis(pentafluorophenoxy) silicon phthalocyanine (F10SiPc) fabricated on a series of methacrylate-based polymer dielectrics containing Polymerized ionic liquids (PIL) units. “Using synchrotron grazing incidence wide angle X-ray scattering analysis, atomic force microscopy, and electrical characterization, we demonstrate that tuning PIL content offers control over F10SiPc orientation on the substrate,” said researchers in the study. “Increasing PIL content from 12% to 65% enables OTFT operation at voltages as low as 0.9 V, with an Ion/Ioff ratio of 104 and transconductance up to 1850 nS. This work emphasizes the importance of the dielectric/semiconductor interface for low VT OTFTs using PILs and F10SiPc.”
