title: Taiwan turns to AI to speed up early warning of Chinese military activity
content: Taiwan is developing a $1.45 million AI system designed to identify Chinese military ships, aircraft and mobile missile launchers in satellite imagery, giving intelligence analysts a faster way to detect changes in People’s Liberation Army (PLA) deployments. The system will scan images covering about 38.6 square miles within minutes, automatically comparing new data with historical imagery and flagging potential military activity. Awarded to Taiwan-Japan joint venture ThinkTron, the project is expected to be completed by the end of April. Rather than adding new reconnaissance satellites, the system will process imagery from existing sources, helping Taiwan improve early warning as Beijing continues to increase military pressure around the island.Speeding up satellite imagery analysisTaiwan’s Ministry of National Defense awarded the contract to ThinkTron through its Communication Development Office (CDO), a military intelligence unit that specializes in collecting and analyzing signals associated with the PLA. The contract took effect on September 25, with completion scheduled for the end of April.The system is designed to analyze multiple areas measuring roughly 6.2 by 6.2 miles, identifying military assets and changes in their deployment. According to sources familiar with the project, it will be able to detect ships longer than about 33 feet, along with smaller targets such as aircraft, missile launchers and mobile radar vehicles.The software will automatically compare incoming satellite images with historical data and flag changes for further examination by intelligence analysts. This could reduce the time and manpower required to search large areas manually, particularly as Chinese military aircraft and vessels operate more frequently around Taiwan.The project follows earlier confirmation from Taiwan’s defense minister, Wellington Koo Li-hsiung, that the military planned to develop a prototype AI-powered satellite imagery recognition system. The main purpose is to help identify potential threats near the island and support decisions about military readiness.The system processes imagery, not satellitesThe $1.45 million contract covers an analytical tool rather than a new satellite reconnaissance network. Military analyst Zivon Wang of the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies in Taipei told SCMP the CDO would use AI to process imagery received from other sources, rather than operate the satellites themselves.ThinkTron, the contractor selected for the project, is a joint venture established by Taiwan’s Sinotech Engineering Consultants and Japan’s Kokusai Kogyo, a geospatial technology specialist. Its existing Tron Eyes technology uses convolutional neural networks to analyze imagery for applications including disaster prevention, infrastructure inspection, agriculture and transportation.Max Lo, executive director of the Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, said the underlying technology is already used by advanced militaries and remote-sensing organizations. The challenge for Taiwan is to integrate it into military intelligence operations and make the resulting analysis useful for decisions in the field.Unlike systems that can analyze imagery directly aboard satellites before transmitting the results to Earth, Taiwan’s planned system will conduct its analysis on the ground at the CDO. That approach still offers the potential to accelerate the process by automatically screening imagery and directing analysts toward changes that warrant closer attention.

title: Humanoid robot Digit 5 targets 20-hour workdays with 9-minute charging
content: Agility Robotics’ next humanoid robot is designed to spend more of the day moving goods and less time plugged into a charger. The company has selected Nyobolt’s battery technology for Digit 5, targeting more than 20 hours of productive work within a 24-hour day.The new system is designed to deliver 90 minutes of runtime from a nine-minute recharge. Early access to robots equipped with the technology is expected in the first half of 2027, serving manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators.The battery upgrade addresses a practical challenge for commercial humanoids: keeping robots working long enough to make deployment worthwhile while limiting interruptions for charging.Nine minutes to rechargeDigit 5’s battery system delivers a planned 10:1 run-to-charge ratio, compared with Digit 4’s 2:1 ratio. That means the newer robot is designed to operate for 10 minutes for every minute spent charging.Agility says the improvement could support more than two full shifts of work each day, helping customers increase utilization across their robot fleets.“For our customers, Digit’s uptime is the business case,” said Daniel Diez, Chief Business Officer of Agility Robotics.“Digit 5 will deliver more than 20 hours of productive work in a 24-hour day, more than two full shifts. That’s the kind of gain that materially improves the value customers get from Digit and the economics of deploying a humanoid robot fleet,” he added. “Nyobolt’s ultra-fast charging technology gets us there, and it’s one of the pieces that makes Digit 5 ready for full-scale operation,” Diez said.Smaller packs, demanding conditionsNyobolt’s high-power battery technology combines rapid charging with a design focused on cycle life and reduced system weight. For Digit 5, the aim is to supply more power from a smaller, lighter battery pack while meeting the demands of industrial environments.“Nyobolt’s technology was chosen because Digit 5 will need more power from a smaller, lighter pack, in environments where reliability isn’t optional,” said Sai Shivareddy, co-founder and CEO at Nyobolt.“Agility set an exceptionally high bar for what a battery has to withstand in live warehouse and manufacturing environments, and this partnership shows what’s possible when ultra-fast charging is engineered for the toughest conditions in physical AI,” he added. The companies position shorter charging stops as a way to support longer operating windows and more demanding task sequences. The announcement does not specify battery capacity or provide a numerical cycle-life rating.Early access targets 2027Agility recently introduced Digit 5 as its first humanoid designed for cooperatively safe work at scale, allowing operation in close proximity to people.Following the initial early-access rollout in the first half of 2027, availability is expected to increase over the next six to nine months.Agility is also preparing to go public through its previously announced combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, with the combined company operating as Agility Robotics and trading on Nasdaq under “AGLT.”For customers, the planned rollout is the next step toward putting Digit 5’s battery performance to work in commercial operations.

title: Scientists Simulated the Universe – And Discovered the Milky Way May Be One of the Best Places for Life
content:
Galaxy evolution in an EAGLE simulation. Credit: The EAGLE project/Durham University
Galaxy simulations suggest the Milky Way offers some of the universe’s best conditions for life, while smaller, more crowded galaxies remain less forgiving.
Earth seems like a troubled place right now, but at least our cosmic surroundings appear peaceful. But this is not universally true, as explosions, collisions, and other dangers lurk in other places and times.
In our new research, published in
Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
, we scoured simulated universes to find the friendliest locations for life.
We discovered something reassuring: the Sun, sitting here in the outskirts of the Milky Way galaxy, is about as good as it gets.
The Goldilocks zones
Regions of the universe that would be friendly towards life are known as habitable or
Goldilocks zones
– they’re just right.
Whether life is actually there is another question. As astronomers and biologists explore how life could form on exoplanets (planets outside the Solar System), astrophysicists follow the structure and evolution of the universe to identify the nicest places, as well as those where life could be snuffed out in an instant.
So, where should we look for life?
The circumstellar habitable zone near a star is ‘just right’ – not too hot, not too cold. Credit: NASA
For example, there is a Goldilocks zone in the
immediate neighborhood of stars
. Too hot or too cold will not do. This “
circumstellar habitable zone
” is just right for liquid water instead of steam or ice.
Zooming out, we can look for the nicest places and times to live in our own Milky Way galaxy. A young star that’s too close to the galactic center will suffer in the hustle and bustle of all the nearby stars, whilst stars that are too far away will be in a sterile environment, devoid of the chemicals essential for life.
Just as Earth is in the Sun’s circumstellar habitable zone, the Sun is in the Milky Way’s “
galactic habitable zone
Let’s zoom out even more. What about other galaxies?
Simulating the universe
We followed synthetic galaxy evolution using the EAGLE (Evolution and Assembly of GaLaxies and their Environments) project – one of the most realistic simulations of the observed universe.
They track the expansion of space, gravity’s pull, and the physics of gas, stars, and black holes, and provide us with a detailed map of what the universe looks like across hundreds of millions of light-years.
With such a map, we asked: where might life be most welcome?
Finding life, avoiding catastrophes
With no observations of alien life, we must make assumptions. The hydrogen and helium produced in the Big Bang are too simple to make organisms, so we focus on generations of stars that have seeded the cosmos with heavier elements essential for life.
Exoplanet observations reveal that Earth-like rocky planets require a certain concentration of those
heavier elements
. However, too much could produce a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that sweeps through the planetary system, eating rocky planets on the way. This is best avoided.
Our breakthrough involves detailed modeling of those things that are bad news for life. Big stars blow up, sterilizing their local environment. Bigger explosions, such as gamma-ray bursts, can fry a much larger volume. Paleontologists think that the Ordovician mass extinction 450 million years ago might have resulted from a nearby explosion.
There are other dangers to avoid. We wouldn’t want another star to wander through our Solar System and disrupt Earth’s nicely circular orbit. So, steer clear of crowded galactic neighborhoods.
Then there are the black holes. Most of these are small and don’t pose any danger, but in the hearts of galaxies lurk monsters. Weighing more than a million suns, these can roar into life as they swallow matter that gets too close. So, stay away as this can result in intense radiation that can strip the atmosphere off your planet.
A home among the galaxies
While we don’t know if life would form in these nice spots, they are the ones that offer the best conditions.
And the results tell us another thing: the Milky Way is rather nice.
This isn’t just a fondness for our own neighborhood. We could have found that life should exist in earlier galaxies, smaller ones, or farther from galaxy centers.
We find that our universe has created plenty of opportunities for habitation, though it seems to be slowing down as the rate of catastrophes catch up with the creation of new planets. Our Milky Way seems typical in the galaxies that have been efficient in turning the raw materials of the cosmos into life-friendly environments.
Similarly, the Milky Way, and its kindred, have put their energetic and dangerous days behind them and settled into a relaxed retirement. These days, even in a billion years of wandering around our Milky Way, less than one star in a thousand would experience an extreme, life-annihilating extinction event.
The story is different for smaller galaxies, which are far more numerous than the Milky Way, as they are too crowded and too energetic.
So, rest easy. And if you get the chance, buying a property in the Milky Way is probably a secure investment, astronomically speaking.
Reference: “Life in the cosmic neighbourhood: galactic habitable zones in the eagle simulations” by Luke A Barnes, Geraint F Lewis, Jaime Salcido, Pascal J Elahi, Miroslav D Filipovic and Richard G Bower, 5 October 2026,
Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

title: “Something out of Science Fiction” – Astronomers Discover a Star That Glows a Bizarre Shade of Green
content:
The white dwarf WDJ1330+6435 appears ghostly green because sodium-rich rocky debris in its dense atmosphere absorbs yellow, orange, and red light. Credit: Mark A. Garlick/University of Warwick
A star’s color usually reflects its temperature, but white dwarfs can break that pattern, with models revealing unexpected shades of green, pink, and purple.
A star that has drawn in rocky debris from its planetary system would appear chartreuse green to the human eye, according to new calculations by
University of Warwick
astronomers. As far as the researchers know, no other star, living or dead, has been credibly identified as green.
The object, WD J1330+6435, is a white dwarf, the dense remnant left when a Sun-like star reaches the end of its life. At roughly 4,000 degrees Celsius, or 7,200 degrees Fahrenheit, it has accumulated rocky material that enriched its atmosphere with calcium, lithium, and sodium.
Dr. Mark Hollands, a Warwick Prize Fellow in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Group at the University of Warwick, who led the study, explained how one of those elements changes its appearance. “The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow. Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star. It feels like something out of science fiction.”
WDJ1330+6435 (green) gets its unusual color from sodium-rich rocky debris, while WDJ0902+2010 (pink) owes its color to carbon brought to the surface by convection. Credit: Mark A. Garlick/University of Warwick
Stellar colors beyond the temperature rule
No white dwarf is close enough for its color to be seen directly, so the team worked from spectra that astronomers routinely collect. A spectrum separates starlight by wavelength, much as a prism spreads sunlight into a rainbow. These measurements reveal a star’s temperature and chemical makeup. For the study, published in
RAS Techniques and Instruments (RASTI)
, the researchers fed spectra into a model of human color vision to calculate how each star’s light would look to our eyes.
“Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like ‘perfect radiators,’ so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs,” Hollands said. “It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me.”
Cooler stars look orange, Sun-like stars look white, and the hottest shine pale blue. The progression resembles iron changing from red to orange to white-hot as a blacksmith heats it. White dwarfs were expected to follow the same temperature-driven pattern. Their name came from the unexpectedly hot examples discovered first, which glowed white or pale blue.
Dense atmospheres reshape starlight
In the coolest white dwarfs, however, atmospheric density can reach about 1 gram per cubic centimeter, comparable to water and millions of times denser than the Sun’s photosphere, its visible surface. Trace elements such as carbon, calcium, and sodium interact with the surrounding dense helium plasma. Those interactions allow the elements to absorb light across a broader range of colors than they would at lower densities, changing the balance of light that escapes.
Color-accurate simulations reveal white dwarfs ranging from pale blue and orange to pink and green. Their diverse colors arise from differences in temperature, atmospheric composition, carbon molecules, and accreted planetary debris. Credit: Mark Hollands/University of Warwick
Across the white dwarfs they examined, the researchers found distinct color groups associated with atmospheric composition. Stars enriched with debris from shattered asteroids and comets, the remains of old planetary systems, tend toward yellow. Cooler white dwarfs with atmospheres containing both hydrogen and helium often appear cyan or pale blue because hydrogen molecules collide with helium atoms under the exceptionally dense conditions.
Carbon-rich white dwarfs are generally pink or purple. One nearby example, WD J1011+2845, may be the reddest star ever recorded. Just 48 light-years from Earth, it has a deep convection zone that has carried carbon from its core to its surface. Carbon molecules alter its light so strongly that almost all of it falls at wavelengths longer than 600 nanometers, giving it a deep salmon-pink glow unlike that of an ordinary star.
The white dwarf WDJ0902+2010 appears pink as convection brings carbon to its surface, where carbon molecules absorb blue, green, and yellow light. Credit: Mark A. Garlick/University of Warwick
Unusual colors in roughly one in thirty
To estimate how widespread unusual colors might be, the team examined a representative sample of the 151 white dwarfs within 20 parsecs, about 65 light-years, of Earth. Five had unusual colors, with two yellow stars and three pink ones. That local proportion suggests roughly one in thirty white dwarfs across the Universe could have unusual coloring.
The other 146 stars were assessed using color temperature, which describes an object’s color by matching it to that of a perfect radiator. The same scale is used for light bulbs, with “warm white” at 3,000 K and “cool white” at 6,000 K. The median for these white dwarfs was approximately 6,800 kelvin.
Surveys selected by brightness can give a different impression of the population. Hotter, bluer white dwarfs shine more brightly and can be detected farther away, making them disproportionately common in those surveys and contributing to the misconception that white dwarfs are typically blue.
Professor Boris Gänsicke, of the Department of Physics at the University of Warwick, said, “One in thirty might not sound like a huge fraction, but across the entire population of white dwarfs in the Universe, that is still a lot of oddly colored stars out there. Yet if we take the median across a representative population of white dwarfs, we found that the average white dwarf really is white.”

title: Scientists Discover a Powerful New Weapon Against a Dangerous Gut Infection
content:
Electron-microscopic image of Clostridioides difficile. Credit: HZI/Manfred Rohde
The promise of an experimental treatment for
C. difficile
gut infections lies partly in the bacteria it leaves alive, according to early laboratory and mouse research.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics can disrupt the gut’s microbial community, allowing a bacterium already living there to multiply unchecked.
Clostridioides difficile
C. difficile
, is naturally present in the intestines of many people and usually causes no symptoms when its numbers remain low. When it proliferates, however, its toxins can trigger acute intestinal inflammation that may become chronic and can sometimes be life-threatening.
These infections, known as CDI, are among the leading causes of antibiotic-associated diarrhea and have high relapse rates. After multiple relapses, patients are often treated with fecal microbiota transfer, commonly called a stool transplant. The procedure is complex and unpleasant for many patients, creating a need for treatments that control the infection while limiting further disruption of the gut’s microbes.
Targeting C. difficile while sparing gut microbes
A team led by Professor Rolf Müller, department head and scientific director at HIPS, has identified a drug candidate that specifically kills
C. difficile
while sparing much of the gut microbiome. HIPS is a site of the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI) in collaboration with Saarland University.
The candidate, argyrin B, belongs to a group of natural compounds identified in soil-dwelling myxobacteria. These bacteria use such compounds to hunt other microorganisms and exploit them as food.
“We were able to show that the natural compound argyrin B is highly effective against CDI: both in laboratory experiments and in a mouse model of the infection, where it significantly reduces the bacterial load,” says Dr. Jennifer Herrmann, a senior scientist in the “Microbial Natural Products” department at HIPS.
Little argyrin B reaches the bloodstream
For argyrins to become medicines, researchers must evaluate both their effectiveness and their pharmaceutical properties, including how they move through the body. When the team gave argyrin B to mice by mouth, very little entered the bloodstream. Instead, it remained largely in the large intestine, where the treatment is needed. Keeping the compound concentrated there could help limit unwanted effects elsewhere in the body, suggesting a potentially well-tolerated approach to treating CDI.
Herrmann also describes how the compound acts against the bacterium and what its selectivity could mean for recovery.
“An antibacterial target of the argyrins had previously been identified and characterized in the notorious hospital-acquired pathogen
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
. Now we have been able to show that argyrin B also acts on this target in
C. difficile
and exhibits particularly high efficacy in doing so. In contrast, the argyrins have virtually no effect on the beneficial microorganisms in our digestive tract. The gut microbiome could therefore be spared during treatment with argyrin and restored to a healthy state more quickly.”
An argyrin-based treatment could reduce the risk of further microbiome disruption, infections, and relapses that would otherwise require a stool transplant. In follow-up studies, the researchers plan to determine the dose of argyrin B that achieves maximum efficacy and use appropriate models to test its effectiveness against recurrent infections.
Reference: “Argyrin B exhibits potent therapeutic efficacy in a Clostridioides difficile-infection mouse model while preserving microbiota functionality” by Sari Rasheed, Katrin Ehrhardt, Ahmed Mohamed Mostafa Abdrabou, Alexander Mellmann, Anna Lechleiter, Domen Pogorevc, Sabryna Junker, Lutz von Müller, Marius Vital, Jennifer Herrmann, Guntram A. Grassl, Markus Bischoff and Rolf Müller, 16 July 2026,

title: Scientists Uncover a Hidden Factor That Could Change How We Manage Diabetes
content:
Researchers found that sleep duration and the timing of physical activity were linked to blood glucose fluctuations, suggesting that when people rest and move may matter more than previously recognized. Credit: Shutterstock
Timing may matter in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes; patients with the steadiest daily rhythms were 2.3 times as likely to meet blood sugar goals, while afternoon activity was linked to smaller swings.
People with type 2 diabetes who use insulin need to keep blood glucose from climbing too high or falling too low. In a study of 122 patients, 46.3% of those with the most stable daily rhythms achieved their blood glucose management goal, compared with 20.0% of those with the least stable rhythms, a roughly 2.3-fold difference.
These daily cycles, known as circadian rhythms or biorhythms, help regulate sleep and activity over approximately 24 hours. Greater rhythm stability remained associated with a higher likelihood of meeting glucose management goals even after the researchers accounted for factors including age, body mass index (BMI), and HbA1c, a measure of average blood glucose over recent months.
Wearables link daily rhythms with glucose patterns
The study involved patients receiving insulin treatment at Ansan Hospital from 2021 to 2024. Participants wore continuous glucose monitors and wearable activity monitors for 10 days, providing records of glucose changes, sleep times, physical activity levels, and heart rates. Pairing the devices allowed the researchers to examine how daily rhythms related to glucose patterns.
A research team led by (From Left) Dr. Lee Da young, Dr. Nan Hee Kim, Dr. Lee Heon-jeong, and Dr. Lee Jung-been. Credit: KU Medicine
The research was led by Dr. Da Young Lee and Dr. Nan Hee Kim of the Division of Endocrinology and Metabolism in the Department of Internal Medicine at Ansan Hospital, Dr. Heon-jeong Lee of the Department of Psychiatry at Anam Hospital, and Dr. Jung-been Lee of the Division of Computer Science and Engineering at Sun Moon University.
“The conventional management methods of diabetes focused on diet, exercise, and medication. But this research showed that we also need to pay attention to the management of biorhythms. Maintaining regular and stable lifestyle rhythms can help manage your blood glucose levels,” said Dr. Da Young Lee.
Sleep and afternoon activity linked to steadier glucose
Sleep duration was associated with both low-glucose episodes and the extent of glucose fluctuations. Patients who got sufficient sleep had a lower risk of hypoglycemia, or low blood glucose, and smaller swings in their glucose levels.
The relationship between physical activity and glucose control varied depending on when patients were active. To examine that timing, the researchers compared step counts with glucose indicators across four periods: early morning, from midnight to 6 a.m., morning, from 6 a.m. to noon, afternoon, from noon to 6 p.m., and night, from 6 p.m. to midnight.
Afternoon activity showed the clearest association with glucose control. Patients who were more active during those hours tended to spend more time within their target glucose range and had less variability in their glucose readings.
Testing whether rhythm changes improve glucose control
The findings establish associations, but they do not show that changing daily rhythms will itself improve glucose control. Testing that possibility will require an intervention.
“Now that we have confirmed the correlation between biorhythms and blood glucose management, we will proceed to conduct a follow-up study to verify whether active intervention in patients’ lifestyles for adjusting their biorhythms would improve their actual blood glucose levels,” Lee added. “Furthermore, we plan to validate the relationship between biorhythms and various diabetes complications such as diabetic kidney disease and retinopathy.”
Reference: “Association of daytime circadian-aligned activity with glycemic control in type 2 diabetes: Insights from continuous glucose monitoring and wearable data” by Da Young Lee, Jung-Been Lee, Inha Jung, Ji A Seo, Heon-Jeong Lee and Nan Hee Kim, 19 February 2026,

title: Scientists Discover a Surprising New Effect of a Popular Blood Pressure Drug
content:
Losartan is a widely prescribed medication used to treat high blood pressure and help protect the heart and kidneys. It belongs to a class of drugs called angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), which relax blood vessels and improve blood flow. Credit: Shutterstock
A drug for high blood pressure could inspire future treatments for people with normal readings, thanks to an unexpected effect on the body’s energy-burning fat.
Losartan already helps people control high blood pressure. New research suggests it could have a second use in activating brown fat, a tissue that burns energy to produce heat and is linked to better cardiovascular health. With a well-known safety profile, the drug could offer a practical way to investigate whether stimulating this tissue can bring health benefits to patients.
That possibility emerged from medical records and PET/CT scans of more than 100,000 patients at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). Researchers noticed that patients taking angiotensin receptor blockers, or ARBs, a class of blood pressure medications that includes losartan, were more likely to have brown fat detected on their scans.
The study, published in
, brought together researchers in Rockefeller University’s Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, led by Paul Cohen, and MSKCC researchers Heiko Schöder and Daniel Lafontaine. To understand what might explain the medication link, they worked backward from the patient observations to experiments in the lab. Cohen’s team has often used this approach, known as reverse translation, to investigate how brown fat works.
Losartan’s metabolic effects follow a separate pathway
When the researchers tested losartan in cultured brown fat cells, the drug directly increased their metabolic activity. It did so through molecular interactions distinct from those responsible for lowering blood pressure.
“The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies,” says first author Nicolás Gómez-Banoy, an endocrinologist and instructor in clinical investigation in Cohen’s lab. “That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure.”
Brown fat cells with mitochondria labeled in magenta. (Image acquired on a CSR Biotech Cell Xtreme microscope on demo at Rockefeller’s Bio-Imaging Resource Center.) Credit: Weslie R. and William H. Janeway Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism at The Rockefeller University
Healthy mice treated with losartan also used more energy, consumed more oxygen, and produced more carbon dioxide, all while maintaining a steady body weight. These experiments support exploring a new use for the drug, although they do not establish that giving losartan to people to stimulate brown fat would improve their health.
Brown fat linked to lower depression rates
The human findings give researchers several connections to investigate. Alongside its links to cardiovascular health, brown fat was associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression, a connection to psychiatric health reported for the first time in this study.
“We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric issues,” says Gómez-Banoy.
The analysis also linked SSRIs, medications commonly prescribed for depression, to reduced brown fat activity. How these observations fit together remains an open question, including whether brown fat itself contributes to the differences in mental health.
Earlier work had focused more narrowly on the heart and metabolism. In
, Cohen’s lab examined roughly 50,000 MSKCC patients and found that those with more brown fat had significantly lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases, including coronary artery disease and type 2 diabetes.
“We only looked for a few diagnostic codes in that study, mainly focusing on cardiovascular disease since that’s what this tissue has historically been associated with,” says Cohen. “The scope of this new analysis is far more expansive. We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights.”
Brown fat’s health links vary by location
The current study also looked beyond whether brown fat appeared on a scan to examine where it was active. The patients had undergone PET/CT scans as part of their cancer surveillance. Focusing on scans that detected brown adipose tissue, or BAT, Gómez-Banoy applied a machine learning tool developed by colleagues at MSKCC to measure its total activity in each patient and its activity in six anatomical regions. These included the neck, armpits, and areas surrounding the heart and kidneys.
Measuring those regions separately revealed that the relationship with disease varied depending on where the brown fat was located. The researchers also compared brown fat with indicators of blood sugar regulation, blood fats, heart function, and inflammation.
“For example, the axillary, or armpit, area was linked to a decreased risk of high blood pressure compared to other regions,” he says. “But overall, patients with brown fat have better glycemic parameters, lipid profiles, and echocardiographic indices, as well as lower inflammatory markers.”
Brown fat was also associated with higher rates of osteoporosis and skin diseases, raising questions about possible downsides. Further research could investigate those associations, examine the genetics of people with high BAT levels, and explore the connection to anxiety and depression.
“There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort,” Cohen notes. “This is just a start.”

title: Scientists Examine 5,000-Year-Old Skulls and Uncover a Disturbing Secret of Egypt’s First Kings
content:
The ancient Temple of Seti I in Abydos, Egypt, stands near the royal burial grounds of Egypt’s earliest kings. Credit: Shutterstock
Serving Egypt’s earliest kings may have carried a deadly cost, and overlooked skull injuries are giving a century-old suspicion new weight.
Some of Egypt’s earliest royal tombs at Abydos are surrounded by hundreds of smaller graves. When Flinders Petrie excavated the site in the 1920s, he suspected that so many people could not have died naturally at the same time. He proposed that members of the royal household had been killed after their rulers died, yet he found no evidence of fatal wounds.
A new examination of 46 skulls from those graves has identified significant cranial trauma in 18 of them. The study, conducted by Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University and published in
Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology
, suggests that at least 39% of the people represented in this sample may have been deliberately killed by blows to the head.
“Retainer sacrifice is a type of human sacrifice where those close to a ruler are killed when the ruler dies,” explained Campbell. “In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler’s power. Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced.”
Skull fractures point to lethal blows
Petrie kept meticulous excavation records but reburied most of the remains, retaining skulls and sending some to the United Kingdom. Campbell located 46 of those skulls in the Duckworth Collection at Cambridge University. Using modern forensic knowledge, she recognized linear fractures as perimortem injuries, meaning they occurred around the time of death. Petrie appears to have mistaken those fractures for damage from natural causes.
A view of the pyramids of Giza, which are approximately 500 years younger than the Abydos tombs, in 1938. Credit: American Geographical Society Library, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee Libraries, shared under the license CC BY-SA 3.0
“The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death,” said Campbell. Some of the 18 injured skulls also showed evidence of sharp-force trauma, including a chopping injury to one individual’s eye.
Egyptian kings are often depicted striking their enemies with a mace, but these retainers were not enemies, and a mace would be expected to leave depressed fractures, with bone pushed inward. Linear fractures generally result from a broad, flat weapon or a fall, so the injuries do not establish exactly how these people died. A fall severe enough to fracture the skull would probably have broken other bones, however, and those injuries should have appeared in Petrie’s photographs or notes.
Officials and artisans beside royal tombs
“I was drawn to these retainers partly because, even though they were buried around royalty, they are mostly relegated to footnotes in the grander narrative,” said Campbell, whose forthcoming book is
State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt
(Routledge Press). “Who were these people and how did they view the ruler and their own role in his or her life and death?”
The funerary complexes were built around 3000 BCE by the First Dynasty rulers, the first kings of a unified Egypt. Alongside the royal tombs were chamber tombs and enclosures probably used for funerary rituals. Smaller, subsidiary burials surrounded both the tombs and the enclosures.
“Each subsidiary burial was a simple chamber in a row of dozens of others,” said Campbell. “Some people had a simple coffin. Most people had a few grave goods, like ceramic vessels, and many graves also included small objects like copper tools, projectile points, or small ivory figurines. Petrie found a few grave markers that had names and sometimes official titles on them. The titles seem to mostly refer to lower- or mid-level officials as well as artisans.”
Some of the other retainers may have died naturally. Others could have been killed by means that leave no skeletal trace, such as asphyxiation, or suffered injuries that could only be detected by examining the rest of their skeletons.
“If I had unlimited resources, I would love to figure out where the bodies of these individuals might be and analyze them!” said Campbell. “Still, this study shows how much new information about the past can be revealed when we revisit previous data armed with updated methods and knowledge, even for datasets that are incomplete and imperfect like this one.”
Reference: “New data from old bones: using bioarchaeology and forensics to reassess legacy data from ancient Abydos, Egypt” by Roselyn A. Campbell, 04 October 2026,

title: The Surprising Reason Some Children Struggle With Math, According to Science
content:
Mathematics is a cornerstone of education, helping students develop critical thinking, logical reasoning, and problem-solving skills. Because math concepts build on one another, a strong foundation early in school is essential for future academic success and navigating everyday challenges. Credit: Shutterstock
Language and reasoning skills help predict math performance, offering clues to the learning difficulties that a test score alone may miss.
Why do some students grasp mathematical concepts with ease while others struggle, even after repeated instruction? The answer may lie in abilities that extend far beyond working with numbers. Mathematics requires students to recognize patterns, interpret information, and apply logical reasoning, drawing on a range of cognitive skills that also support learning in other subjects.
Because math concepts build on one another, difficulties that emerge early can compound over time, making it especially important to understand what drives individual differences in mathematical ability.
A new study published in the
Journal of Intelligence
suggests that language-related knowledge and reasoning ability are among the most consistent cognitive predictors of math performance. Led by Dr. Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in the Department of Educational Psychology at Texas A&M University, the research offers new insights into the mental abilities that support mathematical learning and how educators might better identify students who need additional help.
The researchers brought together findings from 122 distinct test batteries in a single analysis, comparing a broad range of cognitive and academic assessments. A test battery groups tests of cognitive or behavioral abilities, such as the Wechsler cognitive test commonly used to evaluate children’s intellectual abilities. Combining these assessments allowed the team to examine how different cognitive abilities relate to math knowledge, calculation, problem solving, and fluency.
Foundational knowledge of numbers mattered alongside those broader thinking skills. “We found in our study that number sense, which is this general understanding of math and how numbers are related to each other, was just as important and a strong foundation for later math skills,” Hajovsky said. “Cognitive abilities are important for learning and academic outcomes, but it’s not what fully makes up someone’s math ability.”
Making sense of unfamiliar math problems
One of the strongest cognitive predictors, fluid reasoning, involves drawing conclusions through deduction or induction. Deduction applies a general rule to a particular situation, while induction uses specific observations to develop a broader conclusion.
“The example I like to use to explain fluid reasoning is, ‘How well can a student learn a game when there are no prior rules or background knowledge required for it?’” Hajovsky said. “When you’re reasoning internally, you’re still using verbal knowledge and information, but fluid reasoning helps you figure out which information is relevant and what’s irrelevant.”
Language, vocabulary, and verbal reasoning are central to the other consistent predictor, comprehension knowledge. “If someone wants to go to law school, they’ll take the law school admission test. Part of that test requires strong reading comprehension skills and bringing in your own background knowledge or schemas of understanding to make sense of the new information you’re learning. That’s comprehension knowledge,” he said. “It’s important for reading, it’s important for writing, and we see now it’s important for mathematics.”
The link between puzzles and vocabulary
These abilities continue to develop both inside and outside the math classroom through time and effort, Hajovsky said. Their connections extend across tasks that can appear quite different.
“One of the most robust, consistent findings within psychology is something called the positive manifold. Performance on one mental task is positively correlated on a different mental task,” he said. “For example, how well someone can manipulate visual puzzles and mentally turn them is positively correlated with someone’s vocabulary development. They’re both tapping into this mental engine that drives performance on these unique cognitive tasks.”
Mistakes could guide more targeted teaching
Hajovsky hopes that understanding the skills that support classroom success will inform new screening approaches, helping educators identify learning needs early and provide targeted support.
“Instead of looking at a student’s scores, we can pay attention to the pattern of errors they make so we can pinpoint where the greatest learning needs exist,” he said. “In other words, using error analysis to distinguish if math challenges stem from conceptual difficulties like language, reasoning, or efficiency issues and adjusting instruction accordingly. This strategy could be helpful in improving math outcomes for all students.”
Reference: “Cognitive–Mathematics Relations: A Meta-Analysis of Norm-Referenced Standardized Test Batteries” by Christopher R. Niileksela, Daniel B. Hajovsky, Francisco Philippe Cocar-Montenegro, William Joel Schneider, Dawn P. Flanagan and Vincent C. Alfonso, 5 July 2026,

title: Scientists Discover a 99-Million-Year-Old Insect With a Bizarre Feature Never Seen in Living Species
content:
The newly described species: Cretoduros noonoo. Credit: Dolev Fabrikant
Like a bendy straw, an ancient insect’s folded mouthparts may have flexed without collapsing, revealing a feeding adaptation unknown in living planthoppers.
About 99 million years ago, a tiny insect became trapped in tree resin with mouthparts nearly twice the length of its body. The resin hardened into amber, preserving an unusual feeding organ that researchers think could bend through narrow cracks in tree bark to reach sap.
The newly described species,
Cretodorus noonoo
, takes its name from Noo-Noo, the friendly vacuum cleaner in the children’s television series
Teletubbies
. The character’s long, flexible hose resembles the ancient insect’s mouthparts.
Long mouthparts, little evidence of pollination
Noo-Noo belonged to Neazoniidae, an ancient family of planthoppers. In a study published in the journal
, researchers examined fossils from this family, including 13 specimens preserved in Kachin amber from Myanmar. Their living relatives use mouthparts shaped like a simple needle to pierce plant tissues and suck out fluids.
An amber fossil of a Neazoniid planthopper. Credit: Dolev Fabrikant
Although the ancient insects’ long mouthparts might bring a butterfly’s flexible proboscis to mind, the researchers consider that resemblance superficial. Butterflies use their proboscises to drink nectar, whereas Noo-Noo’s mouthparts pointed backward and formed a piercing-and-sucking system less suited to nectar feeding. The researchers also found no convincing evidence of pollen accumulating on the insects’ bodies despite examining numerous fossils. Such accumulations would have supported a possible role as pollinators.
Mouthparts that could bend without collapsing
The elongated mouthparts of the ancient insects were densely covered with crosswise folds. Using high-resolution micro-computed tomography, the team reconstructed their internal structure and found that the folds were part of the organ’s construction, rather than merely surface decoration. Like the corrugations in a bendy drinking straw or flexible hose, the folds likely allowed the mouthparts to bend while keeping them from kinking or collapsing.
Several specimens had their mouthparts preserved in bent positions. Since the resin held the insects in place when they became trapped, the researchers regard these bends as additional evidence that the organs were flexible during life. This folded structure is unknown among their living relatives, suggesting an evolutionary adaptation that has since disappeared.
Illustration of Cretoduros noonoo. Credit: Dolev Fabrikant
The researchers propose that these insects specialized in feeding on tree sap. Their long, flexible mouthparts could have threaded through narrow cracks in bark, guiding the piercing organs toward deeper vascular tissues, which transport fluids through a plant. Two grooved lobes at the tip may have helped secure the mouthparts during feeding. The team thinks these lobes opened against the walls of a crack, anchoring the organ much as a wall plug expands inside a drilled hole.
Thick bark may have favored flexibility
Similar feeding structures appeared beyond this one family. Several unrelated insect groups developed long or corrugated mouthparts during the Cretaceous period, raising the possibility that forests rich in thick-barked trees favored insects able to reach deeper tissues. The study notes evidence of recurrent fires associated with resin-producing Cretaceous forests, and trees in fire-prone environments often develop thicker bark. The researchers cautiously suggest that these conditions may have opened opportunities for feeding strategies now almost entirely absent among planthoppers.
Lead authors of the study. Dolev Fabrikant (right), Dr. Leonidas Romanos Davranoglau (left). Credit: Dolev Fabrikant
The research was conducted by Dolev Fabrikant and Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of the School of Zoology, Wise Faculty of Life Sciences, The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History, and New Environmental School at Tel Aviv University, in collaboration with Dr. Yanzhe Fu of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Davranoglou said, “The discovery of ‘Noo-Noo,’ a new species that lived approximately 99 million years ago, gives us an extraordinary glimpse into the insect world of the age of the dinosaurs. This is not merely an insect previously unknown to science, but an animal that developed an evolutionary solution with almost no modern equivalent: a long, flexible, and durable feeding organ that likely enabled it to reach food deep within tree bark.”
He continues, “The fact that similar structures appeared in several insect groups during the Cretaceous period suggests that ancient forests created ecological conditions and opportunities very different from those we know today. The discovery of a new species like this is therefore not simply the addition of another name to the tree of life, but another piece of the puzzle that enables us to reconstruct what ecosystems looked like and how they functioned tens of millions of years ago.”
Reference: “Flexible Drinking Straws of the Cretaceous: A Novel Type of Labium in Mesozoic Auchenorrhyncha and Its Functional Implications” by Dolev Fabrikant, Yanzhe Fu and Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou, 28 July 2026,
DOI: 10.3390/insects17080789
D.F was funded by a PhD Scholarship from the New Environment School at Tel Aviv University. D.F was supported by the Chinese Academy of Science International Visiting Student program (Project: 132432GJHZ2025011STUPRO).

title: Hurricane Simon Roars Below as Strange Waves Ripple Across the Sky
content:
Hurricane Simon churns off Mexico’s Pacific coast in this image acquired with the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite on October 11, 2026. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
NASA captured strange, rarely seen atmospheric waves rippling high above Hurricane Simon as the powerful storm roared along Mexico’s coast.
Although Hurricane Simon stayed offshore, its powerful winds and heavy rainfall battered parts of Mexico’s Pacific coast, triggering flooding and raising concerns about landslides. Far above the storm, NASA satellites captured an equally remarkable phenomenon: enormous ripples spreading through Earth’s upper atmosphere.
Hurricane Simon became the latest in a long series of tropical cyclones to develop in the Eastern Pacific during the 2026 season. On October 11, the storm approached Mexico as a Category 4 hurricane, with sustained winds reaching 250 kilometers (155 miles) per hour as it slowly moved north-northwest.
Hurricane Simon Brings Powerful Winds and Flooding to Mexico
At approximately 2:30 p.m. local time (20:30 Universal Time) on October 11, the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) instrument aboard NASA’s Suomi NPP satellite captured an image of the hurricane. At that moment, Simon’s eye was positioned roughly 50 kilometers (30 miles) offshore, between the coastal cities of Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta.
National Hurricane Center
(NHC) reported that sustained winds had decreased to approximately 210 kilometers (130 miles) per hour, although the hurricane’s powerful inner core was still moving close to the coastline. Forecasters suggested that the mountainous terrain of the Sierra Madre was helping weaken the storm and reduce the area affected by its strongest winds.
Despite this weakening, Simon remained a dangerous hurricane. Torrential rainfall caused flooding in coastal communities, including the port city of Manzanillo. The heavy precipitation also increased the threat of mudslides in mountainous regions, according to
news reports
Atmospheric gravity waves generated by Hurricane Simon are visible via mesospheric airglow in this nighttime image acquired with the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-21 satellite on October 11, 2026. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
NASA Detects Strange Atmospheric Waves Above the Hurricane
While Simon was producing hazardous conditions near the surface, its influence extended much farther upward. During the early morning of October 11, satellites detected unusual wave patterns spreading through the upper atmosphere.
A nighttime image (above), recorded by the VIIRS instrument aboard the NOAA-21 satellite, revealed atmospheric gravity waves radiating outward from Hurricane Simon. These waves are disturbances in the atmosphere that occur when displaced air moves under the influence of gravity, creating patterns somewhat similar to ripples spreading across water.
In powerful tropical cyclones, the process begins near the eyewall, the ring of intense thunderstorms surrounding the storm’s center. As water vapor condenses, it releases stored energy known as latent heat. This energy helps drive vigorous convection, causing warm, moist air to rise rapidly and form
towering cumulonimbus clouds
The powerful upward motion within these clouds can generate atmospheric waves that travel far beyond the storm itself, reaching the stratosphere and even the mesosphere, two layers of the atmosphere located high above Earth’s surface.
Why These Rare Atmospheric Ripples Were Visible From Space
Although hurricanes can generate atmospheric gravity waves, satellites cannot always detect them. Strong winds at high altitudes may disrupt or weaken the waves before they reach the mesosphere, preventing the distinctive patterns from becoming visible.
When the waves do reach these heights, they can appear as ripples in a phenomenon called airglow. This faint natural light is produced by gases in the upper atmosphere and can reveal subtle disturbances that would otherwise go unnoticed.
The VIIRS instrument includes a specialized day-night band capable of detecting this delicate glow. However, the same sensor also captures moonlight reflected from Earth, which can overwhelm the much fainter airglow signal.
Fortunately, conditions were unusually favorable when the satellite observed Hurricane Simon. The Moon provided very little illumination, allowing the faint atmospheric glow and the striking wave patterns within it to stand out more clearly.
Hurricane Simon’s Unpredictable Path Challenges Forecasters
One possible scenario involved Simon
turning north
into the Gulf of California before eventually making landfall. Regardless of its precise track, the hurricane was expected to generate large ocean swells and dangerous conditions near shore along portions of Mexico’s southwestern and west-central coastlines over the following days.

title: NASA Satellites Reveal a Troubling New Reality in the Arctic
content:
Arctic sea ice reaches its annual minimum extent on September 12, 2026, tying several past years for the 10th-lowest minimum in the satellite record. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
Nearly 50 years of NASA satellite data reveal a troubling decline in Arctic sea ice, raising the possibility of a nearly ice-free summer before 2050.
Satellite observations reveal that Arctic sea ice is covering less of the ocean than it did just a few decades ago, both during the height of winter and at the end of summer. The long-term changes show that the Arctic’s frozen cover is not only shrinking but also becoming younger and thinner.
Each year, a vast layer of frozen seawater expands across the Arctic Ocean as temperatures fall during the polar winter. Ice coverage typically reaches its greatest extent in March before gradually retreating through the warmer months to its lowest point in September. This seasonal cycle has repeated for thousands of years, but satellite measurements show that the amount of ice remaining at both extremes has declined substantially.
On September 12, 2026, Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum (above), covering approximately 4.6 million square kilometers (1.78 million square miles). According to NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), that figure ties the minimums recorded in 2008, 2010, and 2025 as the 10th lowest since satellite monitoring began.
Arctic Sea Ice Is Shrinking and Getting Thinner
Satellites have provided an uninterrupted record of Arctic sea ice growth and retreat since late 1978, allowing researchers to track changes across nearly five decades. Although the overall trend has been downward, the decline accelerated during the 2000s, bringing a succession of record and near-record lows.
One particularly striking pattern has emerged. Every summer from 2007 through 2026 falls among the 20 lowest September ice extents ever measured by satellites. The smallest summer ice cover in the entire record occurred in September 2012.
However, the decline in September ice coverage has slowed in recent years, with minimum extents remaining relatively stable over the past decade. Scientists explain that changing weather conditions can strongly influence how much ice disappears during any particular summer.
Increased cloud cover, for example, has reduced the amount of sunlight reaching Arctic ice during the past decade, helping limit additional melting. According to
NASA researchers
, this has contributed to the recent leveling off in summer ice losses. Even so, September ice coverage remains far below its historical average.
The amount of ice is only part of the story. The Arctic’s remaining sea ice has also become increasingly thin and young.
Scientists have documented a substantial reduction in multiyear ice, which is ice that survives at least one summer melting season. This older ice tends to be thicker and more resilient than ice that forms during a single winter. As it disappears, the Arctic is becoming increasingly
dominated by thinner first-year ice
, making its frozen cover more vulnerable to melting.
The changes are not limited to summer. Arctic sea ice is also failing to recover to its former extent during the winter months. In March 2026, the annual maximum ice coverage statistically tied the March 2025 maximum for the lowest winter peak in the satellite record.
Could the Arctic Become Nearly Ice-Free?
Natural climate patterns have always affected how much ice covers the Arctic Ocean. One example is the Arctic Oscillation, a pattern of atmospheric pressure changes that influences winds and temperatures across the northern polar region.
These natural fluctuations can help explain why ice coverage varies from year to year. However, they cannot account for the persistent decline observed throughout the satellite record.
Instead, scientists attribute the long-term losses to a combination of natural variability and increasing global temperatures, which have contributed to greater melting across the Arctic.
Looking ahead, climate projections suggest an even more dramatic change may be possible. Scientists estimate that the Arctic Ocean could become essentially free of sea ice during at least one summer before the middle of the 21st century.
How Satellites Track Arctic Sea Ice Through Clouds
Monitoring sea ice across the enormous and often cloud-covered Arctic Ocean requires specialized satellite instruments. Scientists use passive microwave sensors, which detect microwave energy naturally emitted from Earth’s surface.
Frozen seawater and open ocean release different amounts of microwave energy, with sea ice producing a stronger signal. By analyzing these differences, researchers can distinguish ice-covered areas from open water and calculate the total area of ocean covered by sea ice.
A major advantage of this approach is that microwaves can pass through clouds. That allows scientists to monitor Arctic ice consistently, even when clouds obscure the surface from ordinary cameras.
The satellite record began in 1978 with measurements from NASA’s Nimbus-7. Beginning in 1987, satellites from the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) contributed additional observations. NASA’s Aqua satellite also supplied data between 2002 and 2011.
In 2025, researchers began incorporating measurements from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s GCOM-W satellite, continuing the decades-long monitoring effort.
The white circle visible at the center of each satellite image represents the “pole hole,” an area near the North Pole where satellite instruments have historically been unable to gather measurements. When calculating Arctic sea ice extent, scientists assume that this unobserved region is completely covered by ice.
Together, these satellite observations provide an increasingly detailed picture of how the Arctic’s frozen ocean is changing, revealing a long-term decline that continues despite temporary variations in the pace of summer melting.

title: Scientists Discover a 100-Million-Year-Old Volcanic System Hidden Beneath Iran
content:
Scientists have uncovered evidence of a previously unknown volcanic arc that formed nearly 100 million years ago in northwestern Iran. Credit: Shutterstock
A 100-million-year-old volcanic arc in Iran holds clues to the history of a vanished ocean whose closure helped shape the Middle East.
An ancient volcanic system in northwestern Iran became difficult to recognize as tectonic deformation, erosion, and burial altered its geological record. Younger magmatic activity during the Eocene further obscured the evidence. Researchers have now identified surviving rocks from a previously unrecognized continental magmatic arc that was active about 101 million to 97 million years ago.
The international team, led by Istanbul Technical University (ITU), calls the system the Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc. Described in
Geoscience Frontiers
, the arc dates to the Late Cretaceous evolution of the Neo-Tethys Ocean. Its remnants lie in a region that is now part of the Arabia-Eurasia collision zone.
Reconstructions of Iran’s magmatic history have largely focused on the Sananda-Sirjan Magmatic Arc and the Urumieh-Dokhtar Magmatic Arc. Recognizing a distinct Late Cretaceous system in the northwest extends that framework and adds evidence for reconstructing the region’s history before continental collision. The wider Neo-Tethyan system connects this history to the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Western Asia, whose geology was profoundly shaped by the ocean’s closure.
Rock chemistry points to ancient subduction
To investigate the arc, the researchers examined volcanic and plutonic rocks from several localities in northwestern Iran, particularly along the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault. Volcanic rocks form from material erupted at the surface, while plutonic rocks form when magma cools underground. Both can preserve evidence of continental arc magmatism, in which an oceanic plate sinks beneath a continent and helps generate magma above the descending plate.
The team used uranium-lead dating of zircon crystals, known as zircon U-Pb geochronology, to establish the rocks’ ages. Hafnium (Hf) isotope analyses helped trace the sources of the magma, while whole-rock geochemistry revealed the rocks’ chemical composition. Together, the results showed characteristics consistent with a continental magmatic arc formed through subduction, the process in which one tectonic plate descends beneath another.
The collaboration brought together ITU researchers and colleagues from the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research and the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, both part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, along with ETH Zurich in Switzerland, Karadeniz Technical University in Türkiye, and Damghan University in Iran.
Dr. Ali Mohammadi, the study’s corresponding author at Istanbul Technical University, explained: “This study shows that the magmatic history of northwestern Iran is more complex than previously recognized. By integrating geochronological, isotopic, and geochemical evidence, we identified a Late Cretaceous continental arc that was subsequently obscured by later tectonic processes.”
A fault may mark an ancient boundary
The arc’s fragmented record provides additional constraints for reconstructing subduction, the migration of magmatic arcs, continental growth, and the closure of ancient oceans. It also raises a question about the fault along which many of the rocks were investigated. The authors suggest that the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault may mark an important tectonic boundary associated with the reorganization of the Neo-Tethyan system.
Changes in subduction may help explain why this magmatic episode was relatively short-lived. Possible contributors include slab rollback, in which the descending plate retreats as it sinks, and arc migration, a shift in the location of magmatic activity. These remain proposed explanations for the development of the Azerbaijan arc as researchers refine models of northwestern Iran’s Late Cretaceous tectonic history.
Reference: “The missing late Cretaceous magmatic arc in the Arabia-Eurasia collision zone (NW Iran): constraints from zircon geochronology, Hf isotopes, and geochemistry” by Ali Mohammadi, Hadi Shafaii Moghadam, Amaneh Kaveh-Firouz, Anna Lechmann, Fulong Cai and Lin Ding, 3 November 2025,
Geoscience Frontiers
DOI: 10.1016/j.gsf.2025.102205

title: 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine Honors Breakthrough That Lets Scientists Control the Brain With Light
content:
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, winners of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Credit: Ill. Niklas Elmehed © Nobel Prize Outreach, CC BY
An algal protein helped scientists reactivate a fear memory in mice, turning light into a tool for testing what specific brain cells do.
Scientists who worked out how to control brain cells with light have won this year’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel were honored for their research into “light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.”
Peter Hegemann, at Humboldt University of Berlin, and Georg Nagel, at the University of Würzburg, wanted to understand how a tiny, single-celled alga called
Chlamydomonas
senses light. Light-sensing is not unique to animals with eyes: organisms throughout the living world use light to detect their surroundings and respond to changes in their environment. Even single-cell organisms have proteins that respond to light. These proteins are used to move towards or away from light, to generate energy, and to respond to the various demands of a 24-hour day.
Hegemann and Nagel
discovered
Chlamydomonas
has a beautifully ingenious mechanism of light detection that relies on a single protein called channelrhodopsin.
Channelrhodopsin is built into the outer membrane of the algal cell. Part of the protein faces the water outside the cell, and part faces the inside. The protein also contains a small molecule called retinaldehyde, which is able to absorb light.
When light hits the retinaldehyde inside channelrhodopsin, it changes shape. This makes the channelrhodopsin protein change shape too. That change opens a tiny passage through the cell membrane. Positively charged particles, including sodium, can then flow from the water outside the alga into the cell. This movement of charged particles sends a signal inside the alga that helps it swim.
Switching selected nerve cells on
How fantastic to have solved such an interesting biological question, but why the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine? The answer lies in the way nerve cells work. Nerve cells use the movement of charged particles (called “ions”) across their membranes to control their activity. When positively charged particles flow into a nerve cell, they can make it more active.
The researchers realized that if they could put channelrhodopsin into nerve cells, they might be able to switch those cells on simply by shining a light on them. That is exactly what Hegemann, Nagel, and the third Nobelprize Prize winner, Karl Deisseroth, a psychiatrist and bioengineer at Stanford University in California, went on to do.
The ability to control nerve cells with light is called optogenetics. It has become a powerful research tool because scientists can use it to switch specific groups of nerve cells on and off and see what happens.
First, scientists deliver the gene for channelrhodopsin to the nerve cells they want to study. The gene is usually carried into the cells by a virus that has been altered so that it cannot cause disease. The cells then make the channelrhodopsin protein, which makes them respond to light.
In animals such as mice, scientists can shine light into the brain through a thin optical fiber. When the light reaches the cells, channelrhodopsin opens, and the cells become active. Nearby nerve cells that do not contain the protein are unaffected.
Light can be aimed at a very small part of the brain and switched on and off extremely quickly. This makes optogenetics a powerful way to investigate how the brain works. For example, if scientists want to know whether a particular group of nerve cells is involved in memory, sleep, sensation, or movement, say, they can switch those cells on with light and see what happens.
Light reactivates a fear memory in mice
one experiment in 2012
, a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology gave mice a mild electric shock in a particular cage. They used optogenetics to tag the nerve cells in the brain’s memory center that were active during the fear-conditioning experiment. Days later, in a different cage, they switched those cells on with light. The mice froze in fear, as if they remembered the shock.
Mice that were not shocked did not freeze, which showed that the light was reactivating a specific memory. Deisseroth was one of the study’s authors.
Early trials seek to restore vision
Optogenetics has transformed scientists’ ability to investigate how the brain and nervous system work. It may also have a future as a treatment. Optogenetics is already in
early-stage clinical trials
for people with retinal degeneration. In these trials, researchers introduce light-sensitive proteins into nerve cells that remain in the retina after the cells that normally detect light—called rods and cones—have been lost. This can make surviving cells respond to light and restore some vision.
Researchers are also investigating whether optogenetics could eventually be used to treat neurological conditions, including
Parkinson’s
epilepsy
This year’s
Nobel prize
celebrates work that started with a question that may sound esoteric: how do
Chlamydomonas
swim toward light? This question has no obvious practical importance. It doesn’t address an urgent need in human health, nor is it a clear route to riches. The success of optogenetics is an illustration of the importance of continuing to ask questions simply to understand the world around us because it’s impossible to predict where knowledge will take us.

title: Perovskite metasurfaces could combine light emission, control and detection in one ultrathin layer
content:
Perovskite metasurfaces could combine light emission, control and detection in one ultrathin layer
Researchers at Dalian University of Technology in China have published a review of halide perovskite metasurfaces: nanostructured surfaces that combine the precise light control of metasurfaces with the emission, absorption and tunability of perovskites. The review covers their design, tuning mechanisms and potential uses in displays, lasers, photodetection and imaging, solar cells, optical communications and quantum optics.
Conventional metasurfaces are usually made of metals or dielectrics such as silicon and gallium nitride. They steer light well, but they lack intrinsic optical gain and are hard to change on demand. Perovskites can fill that gap, since their refractive index, conductivity and emission respond to light, electricity and temperature. The review organizes the field into two routes. In the first, perovskites are combined with conventional metallic or dielectric metasurfaces. In the second, the perovskite itself is patterned into subwavelength structures such as nanopillars, nanodisks or gratings, so that one material both manipulates and converts light.
Among the results it covers, a MAPbBr
metasurface based on bound states in the continuum worked as a vortex microlaser with a threshold of about 4.2 µJ/cm². Metasurfaces integrated into perovskite solar cells have also shown gains: a grating imprinted with a DVD template raised efficiency from 16.71% to 19.71%, and a metasurface blue-light filter let a cell keep 93% of its initial efficiency after 30 hours of illumination, against 41% for the control. These come from earlier studies the review discusses, not from the review itself.
The review also surveys fabrication methods, including focused ion beam and electron-beam lithography, laser processing and nanoimprint lithography. It highlights nanoimprinting as a route to large-area production, with roll-to-roll processes under development, and it covers the
recent progress in perovskite lasers
and earlier
ITMO University work on perovskite metasurfaces
. The authors name long-term stability, scalable high-precision fabrication, optical loss, electrical driving and system-level integration as the main obstacles before the technology can be deployed at scale.
